Note: Reininghaus et al. 2015, Carrière et al. 2015/2019, Adams et al. 2017
(Persistence Images), and the Chazal et al. 2014/2015 series are foundational
PH-feature papers. None are likely worth admitting individually unless we
take refutation 1 seriously — in which case Persistence Images (Adams 2017)
becomes a candidate for fixed-vectorization-of-PH baseline.

## 1912.02164 — Plug and Play Language Models: A Simple Approach to Controlled Text Generation (Dathathri, Madotto, Lan, Hung, Frank, Molino, Yosinski, Liu, ICLR 2020)

**Relevance:** Canonical prior art for the entire activation-steering family that includes ITI (2306.03341), ALS (2509.18116), Brain-Grounded Axes (2512.19399), and our own H-1 / P10-FE1. PPLM does *not* learn a steering direction; it uses gradient ascent on a tiny attribute classifier's log-likelihood w.r.t. the K/V cache `H_t`, with KL regularization to the unconditional LM and post-norm geometric-mean fusion to keep fluency. Directly relevant as the gradient-based alternative to our static-DoM approach: in our terms, "steer with ∇_H log p(correct|H), not with mean(H_correct) − mean(H_incorrect)."

**Key claim we tested:** A 1K-parameter linear discriminator on frozen-LM hidden states is sufficient to steer generation when used via per-token gradient ascent on the K/V cache (with KL/post-norm fluency guards). In our terms: "F-2's probe gradient should outperform F-2's mean-difference direction at correctness steering."

**Our result:** **TO TEST** — H-38 (full PPLM-arm of P10-FE1, BLOCKED on H100 pod) and the cheaper gating sanity checks H-39 (offline single-step gradient on cached prefills) and H-40 (best-of-K reranking by F-2 probe) make the prediction concrete and runnable. Until those experiments report, PPLM is prior art that *predicts* a gradient-steering arm should beat any static DoM arm; F-3's cos = 0.046 is the strongest piece of indirect evidence either way.

**Related experiments:** P10-FE8, P11-FE40, P11-FE41, H-38, H-39, H-40; method-comparison neighbor of P10-FE1.

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **Hₜ-space gradient ascent on log p(a|H)** — single-step or m∈[3,10] inner updates of `Δ Hₜ ← Δ Hₜ + α · g/‖g‖^γ` where `g = ∇_{Δ Hₜ} log p(a|Hₜ + Δ Hₜ)`, with `Hₜ` = all-layer K/V cache up to step t. Per-layer normalization. *Replication cost*: 4h H100 once we have a frozen L19 correctness probe (F-2 already provides one). *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — it's the natural "PPLM-arm" of H-1 / P10-FE1.
- **KL-divergence regularizer to unconditional LM** — adds `λ_KL · KL(p̃_t‖p_t)` to the steering objective during the inner ascent; λ_KL = 0.01 in their main results. *Replication cost*: trivial, ~10 lines on top of the steering loop. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — fluency guard for any steering arm we add.
- **Post-norm geometric-mean fusion** — at sampling time, draw from `β⁻¹ · p̃_{t+1}^{γ_gm} · p_{t+1}^{(1−γ_gm)}` rather than from `p̃` alone, with γ_gm ∈ [0.8, 0.95]. Decouples steering strength from fluency. *Replication cost*: trivial. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — should be standard for any decode-time intervention we publish.
- **BoW attribute model = sum of indicator log-probs** — `log p(a|x) = log Σ_{w∈BoW(a)} p(w|x)`. The BoW arm needs zero training. *Replication cost*: trivial; we don't have an obvious BoW analogue for "correctness," so probably not directly useful — but a *PANL-token* BoW (post-answer-newline tokens that correlate with correctness markers) is a cheap experiment. *We'd plausibly run this*: maybe — only if the discriminator-arm fails.
- **Discriminator attribute model = single linear layer on mean-pooled hidden states** — linear classifier on top of frozen LM mean-pooled embeddings, ~1K params, trained on labeled data (SST-5 in their paper). *Replication cost*: 5min CPU; we already have this for L19 (F-2 probe). *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — it *is* our F-2 probe.
- **Window-of-recent-past update** — to save compute, only the latents in a recent token window get the gradient update (dotted-red region in their Figure 1). *Replication cost*: a config knob. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — at 1024-tok regime, restricting the update to e.g. the last 64 tokens makes the difference between feasible and infeasible.
- **Reranking baseline** — generate r unconditional samples, rerank by `p(a|x)`. *Replication cost*: trivial. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — this is best-of-N on the correctness probe, a useful PPLM-baseline baseline.

### Approaches & framings

- **"Steering = gradient on H, not movement along a fixed v"** — PPLM's central reframing. For our project this is the alternative null to F-3: "the reason prefill_DoM and final_DoM look orthogonal is that we're approximating two slices of one nonlinear gradient field with two linear directions."
- **"p(x|a) ∝ p(x) · p(a|x) sampled by Langevin in latent space"** — Bayesian framing makes the KL penalty principled rather than ad hoc; relates F-2's probe to a generator p(x|correct).
- **"Tiny attribute model + frozen big LM"** — orthogonal axis in the steering literature: scale of the controller versus scale of the controlled. Our F-2 probe is already on the tiny-controller side; PPLM validates this design choice empirically (1K-param linear discriminator suffices to steer 345M GPT-2).
- **"Multiple controllers compose at inference"** — sum log-gradients from independent attribute models. For us this means stacking a correctness probe with, e.g., a refusal probe (H-12) at decode time without any joint training.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **SST-5 (Stanford Sentiment Treebank, 5-class)** — ~12K labeled sentences, MIT, HF. Applicable? no — sentiment is the wrong attribute for our pipeline; we want correctness.
- **Toxicity dataset (Jigsaw Toxic Comment Classification)** — ~160K comments, Kaggle license, public. Applicable? no — same reason.
- **7 hand-curated topic BoWs** (Computers, Fantasy, Kitchen, Legal, Military, Politics, Religion, Science, Space) — 0 cost to construct, public in their repo. Applicable? no for correctness directly; *maybe* for a PANL-token BoW correctness proxy.
- **GPT-2 medium (345M)** prefix prompts ("The chicken", "The horse", etc.) — synthetic, public. Applicable? no — we're on Qwen-2.5 1.5B/7B + MATH-500.

(No new datasets we'd promote into our pipeline.)

### Implementation details worth capturing

- **Reference implementation:** https://github.com/uber-research/PPLM (PyTorch, GPT-2 medium 345M).
- **Hyperparameters used in main paper experiments:**
  - Step size α ∈ {0.02, 0.03, 0.04} (per-layer normalized)
  - Inner update steps m ∈ {3, 10}
  - Norm-power γ ∈ {1.0, 1.5} (denominator exponent in update)
  - λ_KL = 0.01 (works "in general across tasks")
  - γ_gm ∈ {0.8, 0.9, 0.95} (post-norm fusion strength)
  - Window size: short window of recent tokens, exact value not in body — see code.
- **The "weighted-embedding gradient trick"** — to backprop through the discrete-token bottleneck, they use a soft, weighted-sum embedding for the BoW objective rather than discrete sampling. (Cited in author-contribution footnote: "engineered how to obtain workable gradients via the weighted embedding approach.")
- **Per-layer normalization** of the gradient denominator `‖g‖^γ` — important; without it deeper layers dominate updates. Code shows independent normalization per transformer layer.
- **Gotcha:** PPLM does *not* update model weights, but it does require a backward pass through the LM at every generation step ⇒ ~5–15× slower than vanilla decoding at m=3–10.

### Replicable intermediates

- **PPLM-arm of H-1 (= P10-FE1's fourth arm).** We already have: F-2's L19 prefill DoM probe (the discriminator), Pathway 11 1024-tok prefill activations (cached NPZs in `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute/`), and Qwen-2.5-1.5B on H100. Smallest cross-check that fits in cached data: take the existing prefill activations, simulate a one-step PPLM update *offline* on the cached `H_prefill` for the lowest-DoM-decile (F-8 abstained set), re-run the *single forward pass* through L20–L27 (no new generation), and ask the probe at L19 again — if the probe AUROC after one PPLM step is meaningfully higher than before, the gradient direction is at least locally informative. This is a sanity check we can run on existing data without re-generating any tokens.
- **Reranking baseline.** Already implementable on cached K=8 samples (where they exist) — for each problem, score the 8 samples by F-2's prefill DoM probe and pick argmax; compare K=1-greedy accuracy to "best-of-8 by probe." This is a free baseline that should be run before any gradient-steering experiment.

### Cross-paper signals

- **2306.03341 — Inference-Time Intervention (ITI)** — already in graph (status: pending_triage; PAPER_INDEX status: CONTRADICTED partial). PPLM is its conceptual ancestor; ITI is "static head-level vector," PPLM is "per-token full-H gradient." Putting these two in the same triggered-by edge clarifies the spectrum we're navigating.
- **2509.18116 — Adaptive Layer-wise Steering (ALS)** — PAPER_INDEX has it as CITED ONLY but no Paper node in graph. Should be admitted; PPLM is its method-comparison anchor.
- **1909.05858 — CTRL (Keskar et al.)** — NOT in graph. Recommend admission as a CITED ONLY method-comparison: trains a 1.6B-param conditional LM rather than steering a frozen one. Useful as the "expensive end" of the steering-vs-conditioning spectrum.
- **1907.05950 — Subramani et al. "Can Unconditional Language Models Recover Arbitrary Sentences?"** — NOT in graph. PPLM cites it as the most direct prior on hidden-state recovery / steering. Recommend admission as CITED ONLY.
- **Nguyen et al. 2017 PPGN (1612.00005)** — NOT in graph; pre-LLM prior art for "sample p(x|a) ∝ p(x) p(a|x) by gradient steps in latent space." Probably not worth admitting — it's CV.

## 2404.02252 — SMITIN: Self-Monitored Inference-Time INtervention for Generative Music Transformers (Koo, Wichern, Germain, Khurana, Le Roux — IEEE OJSP 2025)

**Relevance:** Direct descendant of ITI (Li et al. 2306.03341) extended
with two additions that bear on our steering work: (a) per-attention-head
logistic-regression probes (instead of layer-mean), trained on individual
head outputs `z_{l,h}(T)`, with hyperparameter-free soft-weighting
`w_{l,h} = ((acc_{l,h} − acc_min)/(acc_max − acc_min))^c`; (b) a
self-monitoring loop that gates the intervention at each generation step
based on whether the probe already reports the trait present
(threshold τ = med(A) − std(A) over top-K probe accuracies). The audio
domain is irrelevant; the head-wise probing architecture and the gated
intervention loop are directly transferable to Qwen-2.5-1.5B activation
steering.

**Key claim we tested:** Two claims, in our terms — (1) per-head probes
have higher signal than layer-mean probes; (2) inference-time
intervention requires self-monitoring to avoid degrading generation
coherence.

**Our result:** **TO TEST** Both claims are tractable head-on tests for
us. Claim (1) is testable on cached prefill activations (H-166, P11-FE205,
~1h CPU). Claim (2) requires the H100 pod and is a clean extension of
the existing P10-FE1 steering experiment (H-167, P10-FE11, 1 day H100).
Until those run, the paper sits as TO TEST. The paper's audio-specific
claims (drums/bass/guitar/piano probe accuracies, MusicGen subjective
listening evaluation) are not in scope for our project.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE205 (head-wise L19 probes, refutation of
F-2 framing), P10-FE11 (self-monitored steering vs P10-FE1), P11-FE206
(self-monitoring replay on cached generations), P11-FE207 (per-token DoM
projection trace). Hypotheses H-166, H-167, H-168.

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **Per-attention-head logistic-regression probes** — Train one
  `LogisticRegression(θ̃_{l,h}, b)` per (layer, head) on the head output
  `z_{l,h}(T) ∈ R^D` at the *last* probing timestep T. Direction θ_{l,h} = the
  trained weight vector; σ_{l,h} = std of `⟨θ_{l,h}, z_{l,h}(t)⟩` over the
  combined train+test probing set.
  *Replication cost*: 1h CPU on cached Qwen 1.5B L19 prefill activations
  (already in `pathway11_h100`).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — direct refutation test for F-2.

- **Soft per-head weighting** —
  `w_{l,h} = ((acc_{l,h} − acc_min)/(acc_max − acc_min))^c` for top-K heads,
  zero elsewhere. Removes the top-K hyperparameter tuning that ITI requires.
  *Replication cost*: trivial — closed-form once probes are fit.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — needed for any multi-head intervention
  variant of H-1.

- **Self-monitoring threshold τ = med(A) − std(A)** where A = {acc_{l,h} | (l,h) ∈ H_K}.
  At each generation step t, compute average probe confidence
  `C̄(t) = mean_h sigmoid(⟨θ_{l,h}, z_{l,h}(t)⟩)`; gate the intervention
  weight per a 3-case update rule (decay/reset/zero) based on whether C̄(t) is
  above or below τ.
  *Replication cost*: drop-in around generation loop (~half day) for Qwen
  1.5B; no new data.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — this is the central unique contribution
  worth porting; it's the "monitor" piece H-1 lacks.

- **Sparse intervention (every s timesteps, s=5)** — Apply ITI only on
  generation steps t ∈ {t₀, t₀+s, t₀+2s, ...}; identity otherwise.
  *Replication cost*: trivial.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — cheap variant for a per-position steering
  comparison; controls the "abrupt change" failure mode SMITIN documents.

- **Probing using last-timestep activation only** — They train probes only on
  `z_{l,h}(T)` where T is the final time step of the 3-second probing audio.
  Discards intermediate-step activations even though they're available.
  *Replication cost*: matches our existing F-2 protocol.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: already in our pipeline — no new work.

### Approaches & framings

- **"Probe-as-classifier *and* probe-as-monitor" duality.** A probe trained
  for classification is reused at inference as a *confidence meter* on the
  running activation. This is a clean reframing: our F-2 probe is currently
  used only as a one-shot prefill predictor; SMITIN treats the same probe as
  a continuous gate. Intersects H-1 (gating signal) and H-13 (per-head
  monitor).

- **Decoupling direction (θ_{l,h}) from strength (w_{l,h}).** SMITIN explicitly
  introduces w_{l,h} as a separate factor from θ_{l,h}, breaking with [27]
  (Li et al. ITI) which folded both into a single vector. This factorization
  matters for H-1 design: we should sweep direction and gate strength
  independently, not jointly.

- **"Generative coherence as a constraint that bounds intervention strength."**
  SMITIN argues (and demonstrates) that audio-LM generation has a stronger
  coherence constraint than text-LM truthfulness, requiring sparser/gated
  interventions. For MATH-500, "coherence" is "valid CoT continuation" — an
  open question whether our regime is closer to ITI (text truthfulness, can
  intervene continuously) or SMITIN (generation collapses if forced too
  hard). H-1 should test both regimes.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **MUSDB** — multi-track recordings with isolated stems; 8.3h drums, 8.0h
  bass; HF-accessible (via mir_datasets). Applicable? **no** — audio domain.
- **MoisesDB** — multi-track audio dataset, 13.1h guitar, 5.7h piano; gated
  registration. Applicable? **no** — audio domain.
- **MusicCaps** (used in text-to-music eval, mentioned in the paper body) —
  HF dataset. Applicable? **no** — audio domain.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- MusicGen-large mono: **48 layers × 32 heads = 1536 heads total**. Compare
  to Qwen-2.5-1.5B: 28 layers × 12 heads = 336 heads. Probe-fitting cost is
  ~5× cheaper for us.
- Hyperparameter defaults: α = 5.0 (intervention strength), s = 5 (sparse
  step), K = 16 (top-K monitoring probes), c ≈ 1 (soft-weight exponent).
- Probing data: 3-second segments, take last-timestep activation. Logistic
  regression on roughly 5–13 hours of audio per trait; balanced classes.
- Threshold τ = med(A) − std(A) where A is the top-K probe accuracies.
- Code: https://github.com/merlresearch/smitin (MERL repo, MIT/BSD-style
  expected — verify before importing).
- Practical observation: ITI without monitoring caused "abrupt change",
  motivating both sparse-step and self-monitoring. Direct port for math CoT
  must anticipate analogous "broken proof step" mode.

### Replicable intermediates

- **Head-wise probe fit on cached Qwen L19 attention head outputs.** Load
  `pathway11_h100/.../prefill_activations.npz`; if it stores residual stream
  rather than per-head outputs, regenerate per-head outputs from the cached
  H100 dump (the 1024-tok extraction kept logits hooks that should permit
  recomputation). Fit 12 probes on prefill, report best-head AUROC vs the
  current 0.7731 layer-DoM. **~1h CPU.**
- **Per-token L19 DoM projection trace, full MATH-500.** Compute
  `⟨θ_{L19}, residual_t⟩` for every t in every cached generation; count
  sign-flip events; correlate with correctness. Tests refutation #3.
  **~2h CPU on cached Stage 2 NPZs.**
- **Self-monitoring gate replay (no actual generation).** Take cached
  generations as a fixed trajectory; at each t, evaluate what the SMITIN
  3-case update would have done to w_{l,h}(t). Tells us whether the gate
  *would* have fired during incorrect-trajectory regions. **~1h CPU.**

### Cross-paper signals

- **2306.03341** — ITI (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023) — already in graph (status:
  pending_triage; PAPER_INDEX: CONTRADICTED). SMITIN's [27]; SMITIN is the
  *immediate descendant* of ITI and is the right comparison point for any
  steering-monitor experiment we run.
- **arXiv:2306.05284** — MusicGen (Copet et al., NeurIPS 2023) — NOT in graph;
  recommend admission only if we ever want a music-domain control; otherwise
  out of scope.
- **arXiv:2306.00107** — EnCodec (Défossez et al.) — NOT in graph; out of
  scope (audio tokenizer).
- **Probe lineage [28]–[30]** (Alain & Bengio 2017, Hupkes et al. 2018, Belinkov
  & Glass 2019) — foundational probing references; not arxiv-IDed in our
  pipeline. Recommend skip; widely cited and not finding-specific.
- Prior music-probe work [31] (Castellon et al. ISMIR 2021) — out of scope
  (audio).

## 2102.11107 — Towards Causal Representation Learning (Schölkopf, Locatello, Bauer, Ke, Kalchbrenner, Goyal, Bengio, 2021)

**Relevance:** Review/position paper introducing the Independent Causal
Mechanisms (ICM) Principle and the Sparse Mechanism Shift (SMS) Hypothesis
as inductive biases for representation learning. Provides a principled
framework for distinguishing *predictive* features (high AUROC) from
*causal mechanisms* (intervenable, transferable, sparse-shift-stable) — the
single most important interpretive question hanging over F-2 (prefill L19
DoM AUROC 0.7731), F-3 (prefill/final-token orthogonality cos=0.046), F-7
(D-bucket signature), and F-1 (universal breathing). Anchors the
causal-vs-anticausal-direction analysis (§VII.A) that gives a fast SSL
diagnostic for the prefill probe; anchors the OOD min-max formulation
(§VII-C) that should gate any selective-prediction publication claim.

**Key claim we tested:** None directly tested yet — paper makes no
quantitative LLM-specific claims. The framework's *implications* for our
findings (sparse-shift-stability of F-3 orthogonality, anticausal-direction
of F-2, OOD-stability of F-8 selective prediction, cross-architecture
universality of F-1) are operationalized as five new FE/H entries
(P11-FE45…111, H-43…110).

**Our result:** **CITED ONLY** (TO TEST via FE107–111, H-43–110). The
paper is a framing piece, not an empirical one — it cannot be REPLICATED
or CONTRADICTED in our experimental sense. What it *does* is sharpen the
interpretation of nearly every flagship finding by giving a falsifiable
test (SMS, anticausal-direction SSL diagnostic, OOD min-max) for each.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE45, P11-FE46, P11-FE47, P11-FE48,
P11-FE49, H-43, H-44, H-45, H-46, H-1 (existing), P10-FE1 (existing),
P11-FE3 (existing).

**Status:** CITED ONLY (motivates 5 new FEs and 4 new hypotheses).

### Methodologies extracted

- **ICM Principle as inductive bias for probe design** — one-line description:
  treat candidate features (prefill DoM, final-token DoM, breathing PR) as
  candidate ICM modules and test mechanism-independence via SMS rather than
  statistical independence.
  *Replication cost*: ~4h CPU on cached NPZs (perturb-and-measure pipeline).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — clean refutation test for F-3 and the
  "two pathways" interpretation; ride on existing P10/P11 NPZs.

- **Sparse Mechanism Shift (SMS) test via prompt perturbation** — apply
  small interventions (paraphrase, numeric swap, distractor injection) to
  prompts and measure how few features in a candidate causal factorization
  move; quantify "sparseness" by ℓ₀ / ℓ₁ ratio of the change vector.
  *Replication cost*: 1 day H100 for re-extraction of perturbed-prompt
  activations on 100 MATH-500 problems × 4 perturbation types.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — discriminates F-3's "independent
  mechanisms" reading from "geometric coincidence."

- **Anticausal-direction SSL diagnostic** — train a label-free SSL probe on
  unlabeled prefill activations (e.g., contrastive on cached representations);
  if the SSL probe improves DoM AUROC, we are in the anticausal direction
  (per §VII.A). If not, we are causal — sharper diagnostic than orthogonality.
  *Replication cost*: 1 day CPU on cached Stage 2 NPZs.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — converts a long-standing question (is
  the probe causal or correlational?) into a one-shot test.

- **Algorithmic-information ICM test (Kolmogorov-style)** — compress prefill
  DoM trajectory and final-token DoM trajectory separately vs jointly;
  ratio ≈ 1 ⇒ independent mechanisms in algorithmic-information sense.
  Practical implementation: gzip on quantized trajectories.
  *Replication cost*: 1h CPU on cached temporal NPZs.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes (low-cost) but expect noisy signal —
  good to bookmark, low priority.

- **Min-max OOD generalization formulation** — instead of single-distribution
  AUROC, evaluate F-2 / F-8 / F-9 over a worst-case set of interventional
  distributions (different MATH subsets, numeric perturbations, prompt
  paraphrases).
  *Replication cost*: 1 day H100 for re-extraction.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — strongly recommended for any selective-
  prediction claim before publication.

- **Disentanglement via SMS as label-free supervision** — use sparse-shift
  signal across naturally-occurring problem variations as supervision for
  factorizing prefill DoM into latent causal axes.
  *Replication cost*: 1 week H100; needs new training pipeline.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no for this project — well outside scope; flag
  as a long-tail item if the project ever pivots to representation learning.

- **Causal-vs-anticausal classification of probing problems** — diagnostic
  procedure to classify any probe (prefill DoM, final-token DoM, CoE-60)
  as causal-direction or anticausal-direction prediction, using SSL
  improvability + intervention-response signature.
  *Replication cost*: 4h CPU.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — meta-level lens on F-2 / F-9.

### Approaches & framings

- **"Statistical model vs causal model" taxonomy (§II + Table I)** — sharp
  distinction between i.i.d.-prediction-only models and intervention-capable
  models. Reframes our probe stack: F-2, F-8, F-9 are currently i.i.d.
  predictors; the project's value-add is upgrading them to intervention-
  capable mechanisms (which is exactly the H-1/P11-FE3 program).

- **ICM Principle as a prior for representation learning** — independent
  mechanisms shouldn't inform/influence each other. Maps onto the F-3
  orthogonality reading: orthogonality is a consequence of ICM but not a
  proof of it. SMS gives the proof-test.

- **Sparse Mechanism Shift hypothesis** — distribution shifts are sparse in
  the causal factorization. Connects to H-9 (breathing amplitude predicts
  difficulty): if breathing is a *causal mechanism* of difficulty, small
  difficulty shifts should move breathing sparsely, not globally.

- **Causal-vs-anticausal directionality of probing problems** — when X→Y is
  the causal direction, SSL is futile; when Y→X (anticausal), SSL helps.
  Recasts the entire DoM-probing program: are we predicting in the causal
  direction (residual → correctness) or anticausal (correctness → residual)?
  Different evidence applies.

- **Coarse-grained causal variables (§VI)** — high-level variables S₁,…,Sₙ
  obtained from low-level X via X = G(S). Reframes B/D-bucket structure
  (F-7) and length-band stratification (H-15) as candidate coarse-grainings;
  validity criterion is whether interventions on S act predictably on X.

- **Modular architecture as ICM prior (§VI Problem 2 + §VII)** — modularity
  in representation as a means to robust transfer. Cross-cuts H-11 (big-to-
  small distillation) and H-13 (head-level attribution): the head-level
  attribution work is essentially asking whether the prefill DoM lives in
  a single head/circuit module (ICM-compatible) or is distributed (non-modular
  shortcut feature).

### Implementation details worth capturing

- **§VII-C OOD risk formulation**:
  R^OOD_{P_G}(g) = max_{P_y ∈ P_G} E_{P_y}[loss(Y, g(X))], where P_G is a set
  of interventional distributions over the causal graph. Useful as a target
  formulation for a "robust DoM probe" objective if the project ever trains
  a probe end-to-end.
- **Anticausal SSL test recipe**: train a label-free contrastive objective
  on unlabeled prefill activations; if held-out probe AUROC improves, we
  are in the anticausal regime.
- **Algorithmic-ICM compression test**: K(prefill_traj) + K(final_traj) ≈
  K(joint_traj) ⇔ independent mechanisms (Kolmogorov complexity, approximated
  via gzip on quantized trajectories).

### Replicable intermediates

- **Algorithmic-ICM compression test on cached temporal NPZs** —
  `pathway11_h100/temporal/*.npz` already contains per-token L19 trajectories.
  Compute gzip(prefill_proj) + gzip(final_proj) vs gzip(concat). Ratio gives
  approximate algorithmic-mutual-information between the two projections.
  ~30 min CPU.
- **SMS prompt-perturbation pilot on existing 500 MATH problems** — using the
  cached prefill activations as a baseline, compare against re-extracted
  prefill activations on a 50-problem subset where prompts have been
  paraphrased (one perturbation per problem, GPT-4 paraphrasing). Measure
  cross-sensitivity ∂(prefill_DoM)/∂(prompt) vs ∂(final_DoM)/∂(prompt).
  ~4h H100 for re-extraction + analysis.
- **Causal-vs-anticausal SSL diagnostic** — train a small contrastive head
  on unlabeled cached prefill activations from the 500-problem set; measure
  whether held-out F-2 AUROC improves. If yes ⇒ anticausal; if no ⇒ causal.
  ~1 day CPU on cached NPZs.
- **D-bucket SMS-stability check** — re-run K=1 + K=8 generation on the same
  500 problems at temperature 0.3 (cached at temp 0.0); compute Jaccard
  overlap of D-bucket membership across temperature. ~4h H100. Direct test
  of whether F-7's D-bucket is a coarse-grained causal variable in
  Schölkopf's sense.

### Cross-paper signals

- **2306.03341 (Inference-Time Intervention / ITI)** — already in graph
  (status: graphed, CONTRADICTED partial). ITI's static-direction assumption
  is exactly the kind of "treats correlate as cause" pattern Schölkopf
  warns against; the F-3 orthogonality + DoM-rotation findings already
  refute ITI's framing in the language of this paper. Connection: 2102.11107
  provides a principled framework for the ITI critique that our project
  has produced empirically.
- **2509.18116 (Adaptive Layer-wise Steering)** — already in graph (CITED
  ONLY). ALS's adaptive layer choice is consistent with the ICM modularity
  prior — different layers as different mechanisms.
- **2604.18805 (Ríos-García, AI scientists)** — already in graph (CITED
  ONLY, motivated H-15). Schölkopf's framework provides the *positive*
  side of Ríos-García's critique: not just "agents skip refutation," but
  "agents conflate statistical association with causal mechanism" — the
  ICM principle is the antidote.
- **2405.07987 (Platonic Representation Hypothesis, Huh et al.)** — already
  in graph (TO TEST, H-20 MEDIUM). The Platonic hypothesis posits a shared
  ideal representation across architectures; Schölkopf's ICM framework
  predicts the same under the modularity prior. Cross-paper triangulation
  candidate.
- **1907.02893 (Arjovsky et al., IRM / Invariant Risk Minimization)** —
  NOT in graph; recommend admission. IRM is the canonical operationalization
  of the §VII-C min-max OOD formulation Schölkopf cites; if the project
  ever runs OOD-robust DoM-probe training, IRM is the baseline.
- **1811.12359 (Locatello et al., "Challenging Common Assumptions in
  Disentangled Representations")** — NOT in graph; recommend admission.
  Direct empirical critique of unsupervised disentanglement that Schölkopf
  cites — our F-3 orthogonality reading should be evaluated against the
  Locatello impossibility result before claiming "two independent
  mechanisms."
- **2007.13916 (Schölkopf et al., "Causality for Machine Learning")** —
  NOT in graph; precursor / shorter version of 2102.11107. Probably not
  worth admitting separately — fully subsumed by this paper.

## 2103.07353 — Computing Zigzag Persistence on Graphs in Near-Linear Time (Dey & Hou, 2021)

**Relevance:** Algorithms paper providing an O(m log²n) graph-zigzag PH primitive. Relevant because F-10 ruled out static VR-PH on residual-stream point clouds but did not test dynamic/zigzag persistence — and zigzag is the natural topological probe for sequence models, where the interesting object is a time-varying graph (hidden states across decoding steps, or attention graphs across layers). The paper provides production-ready code (fzz, C++/Python, MIT) that makes the experiment cheap once a filtration-builder is written.

**Key claim we tested:** N/A on first pass — the paper's claim is asymptotic complexity for graph zigzag PH, not an empirical result we can replicate against MATH-500 directly. The relevant claim *we will test* is downstream: "zigzag PH features on L19 hidden-state graphs across decoding steps separate correct from incorrect trajectories at AUROC comparable to L19 DoM."

**Our result:** **TO TEST** — pending P8-FE4. The current P8 work (F-10) tested only static PH; this paper enables the dynamic-PH test that F-10's scope leaves open.

**Related experiments:** P8-FE4 (primary zigzag PH probe), P8-FE5 (attention-graph zigzag), H-47.

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **0-dim zigzag persistence on graphs in O(m log²n + m log m)** — given a sequence of edge insertions/deletions on a graph, computes connected-component birth/death barcode in near-linear time. Uses Holm-Lichtenberg-Thorup dynamic connectivity data structure and a Morse-pairing technique.
  *Replication cost*: 1h CPU once filtration is built (fzz C++ binary, PHAT/Boost deps).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **yes** — it's the cleanest test of "does dynamic topology beat static topology on residual streams?" which directly probes F-10's scope.

- **1-dim zigzag persistence on graphs in O(m log⁴n)** — pairs negative edges with the earliest positive edges that maintain 1-cycles across intermediate graphs.
  *Replication cost*: same fzz binary, slightly more setup to build the right graph filtration.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **yes** — 1-dim is what would refute F-9 if trajectory cycles carry signal.

- **Alexander-duality extension to (p-1)-dim PH for ℝ^p-embedded complexes** — leverages the graph algorithms above for low-codim PH in higher ambient dimension.
  *Replication cost*: theoretical extension; needs custom code, not in fzz directly.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **no** — residual streams aren't ℝ^p-embedded simplicial complexes; the embedding assumption doesn't fit our setting.

- **Filtration construction via dynamic k-NN graph over a token trajectory** — not in the paper itself, but the natural way to apply fzz to our setting: at each decoding step build a k-NN graph over recently-seen hidden states (or sliding-window vertex set), record edge insertions/deletions as the window advances.
  *Replication cost*: 1d CPU — needs a builder script that converts NPZ residual streams into the fzz `i v1 v2 ... / d v1 v2 ...` text format.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **yes** — prerequisite for any of the above.

### Approaches & framings

- **Time-varying topology as the right primitive for sequence models.** The paper isn't about LLMs but its conceptual move — "deletions matter, not just insertions" — directly targets a methodological gap in our P7/P8 work. We computed PH at fixed snapshots; zigzag PH is the principled algorithm when the underlying object is a sequence. This reframes "is residual-stream topology informative?" from a static question into a dynamic one, with a separate null distribution we haven't tested.

- **Graph-valued time series as the unit of analysis.** Most of our P10/P11 features are vector-valued time series (DoM projections, CoE magnitudes). The paper's primitive is a graph-valued time series — every step is a discrete combinatorial object. This could intersect H-13 (head-level circuit attribution): attention patterns *are* graphs, and zigzag PH over attention graphs across decoding steps is a clean way to measure circuit-level dynamics that's currently outside our toolkit.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- **Code**: https://github.com/taohou01/fzz (C++ with Python bindings, MIT license per repo).
- **Dependencies**: Boost, PHAT (headers must be added to CMakeLists.txt manually).
- **Filtration format**: text file, lines of form `i v1 v2 ...` (insert simplex with these vertices) or `d v1 v2 ...` (delete simplex). Vertices are integer indices, ordered.
- **Output**: barcode = (dim, birth_index, death_index) tuples.
- **Build**: `mkdir build && cd build && cmake .. && make`. Python: `pip install -e .` from repo root.
- **Gotcha**: paper's algorithms are graph-only (0-dim and 1-dim); higher-dim PH on simplicial complexes still pays the O(m^ω) general cost. For our use case the graph case is the right one.
- **Scaling**: m = filtration size (total insertions+deletions). For a 1024-token trajectory with k=5 NN graph and sliding window 50, filtration size is ~50k. fzz handles 10⁶ trivially.

### Replicable intermediates

- **0-dim zigzag PH on a single MATH-500 trajectory** (sanity check, ~2h CPU): pick one correct + one incorrect 1.5B trajectory from `pathway11_h100/` cached L19 NPZs, build sliding-window k=5 NN graph (window=50 tokens), emit fzz filtration file, run binary, plot 0-dim barcode. Goal: confirm barcodes are non-trivial (multiple intervals) and visually distinct between correct/incorrect on a *single* example before scaling up.
- **Static-vs-zigzag null comparison** (~4h CPU): on the same trajectories, run static VR-PH on the union of all hidden states (the F-10 setup) and zigzag PH on the temporal filtration. If static is at Gaussian null but zigzag isn't, F-10 reading narrows.
- **Build script reusability**: the NPZ → fzz-filtration converter is the only new code; it can be reused for H-13 (attention-graph zigzag) and H-22 (abstract-CoT zigzag) without modification.

## 2103.14743 — Outlier-robust subsampling techniques for persistent homology (Stolz, 2021/JMLR-style preprint, revised 2022)

**Relevance:** Pure methodology paper for noisy point-cloud PH on synthetic 3D/4D datasets (sphere, torus, Klein bottle). Bears on the project at exactly one but high-leverage point: the landmark-selection step that sits behind every PH computation in Pathway 8 and the F-10 verdict. Stolz documents that random subsampling biases toward dense regions and maxmin includes outliers — both of which can collapse genuine sparse topological signal to a Gaussian-null reading without that being the truth. Provides a per-point local-PH score (`out_PH^{0,1,2}`, `out_PH^1`) that is also reusable as a candidate D-bucket detector and a non-density alternative to H-7's mechanism.

**Key claim we tested:** That random/maxmin landmark subsampling can fabricate "no-topology" verdicts on noisy point clouds where a topology-aware (local-PH-driven) subsampling reveals genuine signal.

**Our result:** **TO TEST**. F-10 (PH at Gaussian null on residual streams) used standard random/maxmin subsampling and was treated as definitive; Stolz makes that landmark choice non-trivially refutable. Two cheap experiments queued (P8-FE6 to re-test F-10 under PH-landmarks; P11-FE50 to test PH-outlierness as a per-point D-bucket detector against H-7's density mechanism).

**Related experiments:** P8-FE6, P8-FE7, P11-FE50, H-48, H-49. Tangential to F-2/F-3/F-8 (no directional-probe content in the paper).

**Status:** TO TEST (H-48 MEDIUM, H-49 MEDIUM).

### Methodologies extracted

- **PH-outlierness `out_PH^{0,1,2}(y)` and `out_PH^1(y)`** — per-point score equal to the longest finite bar in the local Vietoris–Rips persistence barcode (over dims 0+1+2 or restricted to dim 1 only) computed inside a δ-neighbourhood of `y`.
  *Replication cost*: ~1h CPU on cached Pathway 11 prefill L19 residuals (Ripser on N=500 δ-balls is parallelisable and trivially cheap per ball).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — cheapest possible refutation channel for F-10, F-7, H-7, and the score is reusable as a feature in any future probe.

- **PH landmarks I (representative, low-outlierness points)** — Algorithm 1; subsample via lowest `out_PH(y)`.
  *Replication cost*: subset of (1) above; same cost.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly tests R1 by re-running F-10 PH after PH-landmark subsampling.

- **PH landmarks II (vital, high-outlierness points)** — opposite of above; high-outlierness points retained.
  *Replication cost*: subset of (1).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — Stolz hypothesises this is the better choice in high dimension; we should test the dim-1-restricted version specifically on residual streams.

- **Super-outlier flag** — points with <2 neighbours in their δ-ball; held back from landmark set unless quota forces inclusion.
  *Replication cost*: trivial.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — nice diagnostic for "isolated" residuals; might catch D-bucket members directly.

- **k-- landmarks (modified k-means--, Chawla & Gionis 2013)** — outlier-robust k-means variant adapted to landmark selection by selecting the data point closest to each cluster centre.
  *Replication cost*: ~30min CPU.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no — paper itself reports k-- only outperforms baselines at high sampling density (which we wouldn't be in for residual streams) and cost dominates the PH-landmark route.

- **Local Vietoris–Rips with bounded δ-neighborhood** — sidesteps the global O(2^N) blowup by computing PH only on simplices contained in a δ-ball.
  *Replication cost*: trivial — Ripser handles it.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — the only computationally feasible PH computation on 1024-tok residual clouds at meaningful δ.

### Approaches & framings

- **"Landmark selection should preserve topology, not coverage."** Reframes the standard `de Silva & Carlsson 2004` desiderata (good coverage + even spacing) by saying: in the PH context, the *only* thing that matters is whether the landmark subset preserves the persistent homology of the full cloud. This is a useful frame for any future writeup of F-10 — F-10's null verdict is only as good as the topology-preservation guarantee of its landmark scheme, and we have not stress-tested that.
- **"Mayer–Vietoris bound on per-point inclusion/exclusion."** Per-point importance to global topology can be quantified by the size of the local link's PH. This is a *new lens* for D-bucket detection (per-point) that is otherwise not reusable in our pipeline.
- **"Outlier-robustness as a statable goal for PH preprocessing."** Most PH papers we have triaged so far (F-10's references, Wheeler et al. 2021) treat noise as a regularity issue at the persistence-stability level, not at the subsampling level. This paper says: the choice of landmark *is* the outlier-robustness lever, and existing PH-on-NN papers have not even noticed.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **Sphere-cube, sphere-plane, sphere-line, sphere-Laplace-line, torus, Klein bottle** — synthetic, 3D and 4D, 3000 points each, varied signal/noise probability `p`.
  Size: 3000 points × 3-4 dim. License: trivially synthetic. Accessibility: regenerate from formulas in §4.
  Applicable? no for residual-stream content, **yes** as a sanity-check sandbox: before applying PH-outlierness to 1024-tok residuals, replicate Stolz's sphere-cube case study to validate our Ripser pipeline and δ-tuning.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- Author's reference implementation: Matlab + Ripser (Bauer 2021).
- `δ` is the only knob; smaller `δ` gives sharper results in their experiments. Recommended default in §5.1: `δ ≈ 0.2` on unit-sphere-scale data — for our residual streams we'd need to rescale to median nearest-neighbour distance.
- Two outlierness flavours: `out_PH^{0,1,2}` (max over all dims; in their data this is dominated by dim 0) and `out_PH^1` (dim-1 only, more semantic). For high-dim data Stolz explicitly recommends `out_PH^1` (Discussion §6).
- "Super-outlier" gating: any point with <2 neighbours in its δ-ball is held back from the landmark set unless quota forces inclusion. Implementation gotcha: Stolz randomly permutes ties (points with `out_PH^1=0`) to avoid systematic ordering effects from input data ordering — we have to do the same or our Pathway 11 numpy index order will leak into landmark choice.
- No public code repo cited — just "Matlab + Ripser". We'd reimplement in Python (gudhi or ripser.py) which is straightforward.
- Algorithm 1 is the canonical pseudocode; Algorithm 2 is k-- modified for landmark selection. Both reproduced in the paper body.

### Replicable intermediates

- `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute/extracts/` (or equivalent Stage 2 NPZ) — already-cached prefill L19 residuals on the 1.5B MATH-500 K=1 set. Run `out_PH^1(y)` per problem at scaled-δ. Single 1h CPU job.
- `pathway8_layerwise/` outputs (the F-10 source) — re-run the same persistence pipeline used there but swap the landmark step for Algorithm 1 (`PH landmarks I` and `PH landmarks II`). Produces a directly comparable persistence diagram alongside the existing Gaussian baseline. Cost: 2h CPU because we'd need to land-mark + persist 28 layers.
- `validate_claims.py` does not need updating — this brief introduces no new quantitative claims (yet); the experiments above will produce them.

### Cross-paper signals

- **2509.26560 (Chun et al., Estimating Dimensionality from Finite Samples)** — already in graph (status: TO TEST under H-16). Both papers attack the *same* failure mode — that finite-sample noise on high-dim point clouds biases topological/dimensional summaries — but from orthogonal directions: Chun corrects PR via Marchenko–Pastur, Stolz robustifies PH subsampling. Pairing them would be a stronger H-16/H-Stolz joint test than either alone.
- **Wheeler et al. 2021** (NN topological complexity layer-by-layer, cited in §1) — NOT in graph. Looks like a direct precursor to F-10 / Pathway 8 layer-wise PH and worth admitting. Recommend: `link-forge` admit and re-triage.
- **Skraba & Turner 2020** (Wasserstein stability of Vietoris–Rips on finite point clouds) — NOT in graph. Provides the formal stability bound that justifies PH-as-a-correctness-signal at all; relevant when writing up F-10 properly.
- **Cohen-Steiner et al. 2007** (Stability of persistence diagrams) — foundational; NOT in graph. Should be a CITED ONLY entry whenever any PH finding gets a writeup.
- **Bendich et al. 2012, Fasy & Wang 2016, Ahmed et al. 2014** — local-PH precursors, NOT in graph; lower priority for admission unless we end up writing up D-bucket-as-local-PH-anomaly.
- **de Silva & Carlsson 2004** (lazy witness filtration, original maxmin algorithm) — NOT in graph; foundational for any PH writeup.

## 2106.00012 — Persistent Homology Captures the Generalization of Neural Networks Without A Validation Set (Gutiérrez-Fandiño et al., 2021)

**Relevance:** Concurrent prior-art for F-10. Paper claims PH *does* track generalization, but on a different object (between-state Heat-distance over MLP weight-graph PDs) than F-10 tested (within-state H0/H1 features over residual-stream point clouds). The objects differ enough that F-10 isn't directly contradicted; the comparison is a method-difference axis (CONTRADICTED_BY with `method_differs=true` annotation in the graph). Still, three of the paper's choices (giotto-tda Heat / Silhouette vectorization, η=0.01 lifespan filter, between-state distance framing) are concrete cheap upgrades to EXP-026 that could close or widen the F-10 null gap.

**Key claim we tested:** Heat-distance between persistence diagrams of consecutive neural-network states correlates with validation accuracy (Pearson 0.62–0.89 across MLPs, 0.42–0.61 on CNNs).

**Our result:** **TO TEST.** The closest available cross-check is to upgrade EXP-026 with the paper's preferred PD-vectorization (P11-FE51) and lifespan filter (P11-FE53), and to apply the between-state framing across tokens within MATH-500 problems (P11-FE52). None of these are run yet.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE51, P11-FE52, P11-FE53, P11-FE54; H-50, H-51, H-52.

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **Directed flag complex on weighted MLP edge-graph.** Each neuron is a 0-simplex; edges are weighted by `max(1 − |w|/max(|W|), ζ)` with ζ=1e-6 (Eq. 1). Negative weights become reverse edges, biases become edges to isolate vertices. *Replication cost*: 20–30 min CPU for a Qwen-1.5B head module per checkpoint; full model is intractable per their 7-day-on-2×V100 estimate. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes for *probe-head* MLPs only (cheap), no for full Qwen weights (memory-bound, paper authors flag scalability as the headline limitation).
- **Edge-weight–thresholded filtration with normalized weight ∈ [0,1].** ε sweeps 0→1 with η=0.01 minimum interval to suppress noise; persistence intervals computed up to H3 over Z2. *Replication cost*: 1–2h CPU per persistence diagram on a small MLP. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes for ablation against Pathway 9's H0+H1-only setup.
- **Heat and Silhouette PD vectorizations (giotto-tda).** Discretized form of PD permits efficient distance computation across millions of intervals; paper picks Heat over Silhouette empirically (Heat plots cleaner). *Replication cost*: trivial wrapper around existing giotto-tda calls. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — direct upgrade for the EXP-026 PH features (currently uses raw H0_max_lifetime, H0_entropy, H1_pers_entropy, etc., not vectorizations).
- **Between-consecutive-state PD distance ("homological convergence").** Compute PD at state t and t+1, take Heat-distance. *Replication cost*: 1–2h CPU per consecutive pair. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — analogue for between-token residual streams is the most novel reusable framing.
- **Cumulative-vs-non-cumulative distance summary.** Cumulative integration of step-wise distances stabilizes the curve enough to compare with val-acc. *Replication cost*: trivial. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes if we adopt the between-state framing.
- **Persistence diagram filtering by interval lifespan η.** Drop intervals with `death − birth < 0.01`. *Replication cost*: trivial. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly applicable to EXP-026 features.

### Approaches & framings

- **Homological convergence as a holdout-free generalization monitor.** Reframes generalization tracking as a *self-similarity* problem (compare model to itself across training) rather than an *external-data* problem (compare model output to held-out labels). Intersects F-10 (which tested *within-state* PH and got null) by suggesting we tested the wrong object.
- **Between-state vs within-state TDA dichotomy.** Most TDA-on-NN papers measure within-state structure (one PD per network); this paper measures between-state evolution (Δ-PD per step). Reframes F-9's "trajectory features are redundant" — depth-trajectory ≠ time-trajectory.
- **Architecture-coupling of PH-on-weights.** Their CNN failure mode (r=0.42) makes architecture-dependence explicit. Intersects F-1's universality framing by carving out a regime (conv weights) where their method fails but breathing presumably wouldn't.
- **PH as a scale-up wall.** Authors flag 7 days on 2×V100 for tiny MLPs (4–256 unit layers) on MNIST/CIFAR. This is a hard scaling cliff, and means "PH on Qwen weights" is methodologically blocked, motivating activation-space alternatives (which is what F-10 already explored).

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **MNIST** — 70k samples, public, HF-equivalent. Applicable? **no** — small-MLP regime, no token sequences.
- **CIFAR-10 / CIFAR-100** — 60k samples each, public. Applicable? **no** — vision, not relevant to MATH-500/CoT.
- **Reuters** — multi-label text classification (~10.7k docs), Apache-2.0. Applicable? **no directly**, but interesting sole text-classification baseline (r=0.62 — lowest MLP correlation, possibly because Reuters labels are noisier).

### Implementation details worth capturing

- Code: https://github.com/asier-gutierrez/nn-evolution (MIT)
- Library: giotto-tda (PD vectorizations, distance computations)
- Filtration normalization: `max(1 − |w|/max(|max(W)|, |min(W)|), ζ)`, ζ=1e-6
- Persistence interval filter: η=0.01 minimum lifespan, infinity replaced by 1.0
- Field: Z₂ for persistence
- Homology dimensions: H0–H3
- Optimizer for MLPs: RMSProp, batch 256
- Architectures: base MLP `{Input, Linear(512), Dropout(0.2), Linear(512), Dropout(0.2), Output}`; CNN feature extractor frozen (3 conv blocks, k=3, starting 32 channels, max-pool interleaved)
- Hyperparameter sweeps: layer size {4,16,32,128,256}, label count {2,4,6,8,10}, lr {1e-5..0.1}, dropout {0,0.2,0.4,0.5,0.8}; 5 seeds each
- Hardware: 2×V100 32GB + 1.5TB RAM, 7 days

### Replicable intermediates

- **Add Heat / Silhouette vectorization to EXP-026 PH feature pipeline.** Pathway 9 currently uses raw H0/H1 summary stats (max_lifetime, entropy, n_features). Re-running with giotto-tda's Heat/Silhouette-distance-to-reference-PD as a feature is ~1h CPU on cached 1.5B L19 activations, would directly test whether the 0.690 vs 0.693 null gap closes under the paper's exact discretization choice. Cached artifact: `pathway9/results/exp3a_gaussian_null_v2.json` + `pathway9/cache/L19_qwen15b_*.npz`.
- **Pairwise inter-problem PD-Heat distance matrix on cached L19 prefill activations.** Use the 500 MATH-500 prefill activations (cached for F-2's 0.7731 AUROC) and compute pairwise Heat-distance between problem-PDs. If the matrix has block structure aligned with correctness, that's a per-problem replication of the paper's between-state framing applied across-problem. ~2h CPU. Cached artifact: `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute/prefill_activations.npz` (per DATA_MANIFEST).
- **Apply η=0.01 lifespan filter to existing PH features.** Re-compute Pathway 9 features after dropping intervals with lifespan < 0.01 (currently no filter). Trivial code change, may shift the 0.690 number. Cached artifact: same as EXP-026.

### Cross-paper signals

- **1812.09764** — already in graph (status: pending_triage; a concurrent triage brief exists per `briefs/triage-2026-04-29-1812.09764.md` in repo). Rieck et al. "Neural Persistence" — the paper's [26] reference; another PH-on-weights complexity measure but for *static* networks rather than between-state.
- **1802.04443** — already in graph (status: pending_triage; concurrent brief exists). Guss & Salakhutdinov — paper's [13]/[14], capacity of NN via algebraic topology; cited by the paper as the prior-art reformulation they extend.
- **1810.00113** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Jiang et al. "Predicting the Generalization Gap in Deep Networks with Margin Distributions" — directly comparable holdout-free generalization predictor; both the present paper and our F-2/F-8 are different answers to the same question.
- **2002.04805** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Hofer et al. "Topologically Densified Distributions" — uses PH as a *training* loss; F-1 / H-10 comparison point for whether PH-aware training changes breathing.

## 2111.13171 — Intrinsic Dimension, Persistent Homology and Generalization in Neural Networks (Birdal, Lou, Guibas, Şimşekli, 2021)

**Relevance:** NeurIPS 2021 paper that introduces "persistent homology
dimension" (PHD) as an unsupervised scalar fractal-dimension estimator and
proves a generalization bound in terms of PHD applied to the **SGD trajectory
in parameter space** (1000-step sliding window of weight snapshots). The bound
itself does NOT apply to our setting (frozen-weights, per-input activation
geometry) — Birdal's point cloud is `(W_t)_{t=1..1000} ∈ R^{#params}`, ours is
`(h_i)_{i=1..1024} ∈ R^{1536}`. However, the **PHD estimator algorithm**
(`calculate_ph_dim`: log-regression of PH-0 sum-of-bar-lifetimes against
subsample size) is fully reusable as a different-statistic re-test of F-10
nullity and as a label-free correctness probe candidate against F-2/F-8.

**Key claim we tested:** That PHD-via-log-regression is a more sensitive
fractal-dimension estimator than fixed-scale PH fingerprints, and that PHD
applied to a sufficiently large point cloud (~1000 points) is informative
about that cloud's geometry.

**Our result:** **TO TEST.** Birdal's algorithm has not yet been run against
our cached residual-stream point clouds. The natural tests are P7-FE3 (re-run
F-10 with `calculate_ph_dim`) and P11-FE55 (per-problem PHD-AUROC against K=1
correctness). The Birdal bound itself is object-mismatched and CITED ONLY for
the bound; the algorithm is TO TEST.

**Related experiments:** P7-FE3, P11-FE55, P11-FE56; H-53, H-54, H-55.

**Status:** TO TEST (algorithm portion); CITED ONLY (bound — object mismatch).

### Methodologies extracted

- **PHD scaling-law estimator (`calculate_ph_dim`)** — given point cloud `W`,
  log-uniformly subsample sizes `n_1, …, n_K`; for each `n_k` draw a random
  subset, run Vietoris-Rips on its pairwise distance matrix, take PH-0 only,
  sum bar lifetimes `E_k = Σ (death − birth)`; regress `log E_k ~ log n_k`,
  estimate slope `m`, output PHD = `1 / (1 − m)`. Defaults: `min_points=200`,
  `max_points=1000`. CPU via `ripser`; differentiable GPU via `TorchPH`.
  *Replication cost*: 20 min CPU on a 1024×1536 prefill cloud.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **yes** — drop-in replacement for our
  PH-on-residuals probe at near-zero cost.

- **Sliding-window trajectory tracking** — maintain a deque of 1000 weight
  snapshots during SGD; re-estimate PHD per window for trajectory-level
  generalization monitoring.
  *Replication cost*: requires from-scratch training.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **no** — we don't train models from scratch in
  this program; doesn't apply to frozen-Qwen pipeline.

- **Differentiable PHD regularizer** — TorchPH backend allows PHD as an
  end-to-end training loss term, regularizing toward lower fractal dimension.
  *Replication cost*: requires training run with PHD loss.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **no** — same reason as above.

### Approaches & framings

- **Generalization as a property of the SGD trajectory, not final weights** —
  connects to our breathing framing: both treat the *dynamic* (training
  trajectory or per-token activation trajectory) as the carrier of meaningful
  geometry, rather than a static snapshot. This is consonant with H-4
  (breathing ↔ EoS) and the chain-of-embedding (CoE) family.
- **Multi-scale PH as a fractal-dimension estimator** — reusable framing for
  P7/P8 work: instead of single-scale PH features, treat sum-of-PH-0-lifetimes
  vs subsample-size as a signal. This is what F-10's nullity test missed.
- **Object-level care about *what* the point cloud is** — Birdal is explicit
  that PHD bounds generalization only when the point cloud is the SGD
  trajectory. Useful framing for our PAPER_INDEX hygiene: every PH-on-
  neural-net paper should be classified by what point cloud it operates on
  (params vs activations vs attention).

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **MNIST** — small, image classification. Not applicable to MATH-500.
- **CIFAR-10 / CIFAR-100** — image classification. Not applicable.

(All experiments are vision-classification training-from-scratch; nothing
transfers to our pretrained-LLM, math-reasoning, frozen-weights regime.)

### Implementation details worth capturing

- Code: `https://github.com/tolgabirdal/PHDimGeneralization` (MIT, 4 commits).
- `topology.py:calculate_ph_dim(W, min_points=200, max_points=1000, h_dim=0)` —
  drop-in CPU function; depends on `ripser`. Output: scalar PHD.
- `calculate_ph_dim_gpu` requires `TorchPH` (https://github.com/c-hofer/torchph)
  if differentiability needed; not needed for our probe-only application.
- Default subsample-size schedule is 7 log-spaced points between 200 and 1000.
- The estimator is invariant to ambient embedding dimension *as long as the
  intrinsic dimension is far smaller* — important for L19 residuals (1536-dim
  ambient, expected ID much smaller).
- Architecture choices in original paper (FCN/AlexNet/VGG) are irrelevant to
  us; only `topology.py` is reusable.

### Replicable intermediates

- **F-10 re-test**: load cached pathway 8 layer-wise residual NPZ for L19,
  randomly subsample K=20 problems × 1024 tokens each, run
  `calculate_ph_dim(W)`, compare against PHD on a Gaussian point cloud of
  matched shape. ~30 min CPU. Cached artifact: `pathway8_layerwise/*.npz`.
- **F-7 per-problem PHD probe**: load `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute`
  Stage 2 prefill L19 NPZ (1024×1536 per problem × 500 problems), compute
  per-problem PHD, stratify by A/B/C/D bucket from pathway 11 result JSON.
  ~30 min CPU. Cached artifact: `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute/results.json`
  (for bucket labels) + Stage 2 NPZs (gitignored, regen recipe in
  DATA_MANIFEST).
- **F-2 label-free competitor**: same as above, but compute AUROC against the
  K=1 correctness column in `results.json` instead of bucket labels. Direct
  comparison to 0.7731 anchor.

### Cross-paper signals

- **2103.07353** — already in graph (status: pending_triage). Fast Zigzag
  Persistence (Dey-Hou). Adjacent methodological tooling — could be combined
  with Birdal-style PHD scaling but on temporal point clouds.
- **2410.11042** — already in graph (status: pending_triage). Persistent
  Topological Features in LLMs. Activation-space PH; complementary point-cloud

- **2509.26560** — already in graph (status: pending_triage). Estimating
