## 2412.15296 — Confidence in the Reasoning of Large Language Models (Pawitan & Holmes, 2024)

**Relevance:** Pessimistic empirical study of LLM self-confidence on
non-math reasoning tasks (causal judgment, formal fallacies,
probability puzzles) using closed-source models (GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo,
Mistral). Stays purely at the prompt-output level — no hidden-state
or residual-stream probing. Headline conclusion: "current LLMs do not
have any internally coherent sense of confidence" — second-pass
accuracy is often worse than first-pass, verbal confidence is
overstated, and verbal confidence is only partially explained by
token-level probability. Bears on F-2 (cross-domain generality of
prefill DoM AUROC), F-8 (selective-prediction recoverability premise),
and H-12 (label-free internal coherence assumption).

**Key claim we tested:** That LLM confidence — verbal, behavioral, and
token-probability — is incoherent across tasks; reconsideration
worsens accuracy; calibration is poor.

**Our result:** **TO TEST** (CITED ONLY pending H-284/H-285/H-286). The
paper does not directly evaluate residual-stream-based confidence
signals (which is our project's only confidence channel). Our prefill
DoM (F-2) is a *different* probe than verbal/persistence/token-prob
confidence and has only been measured on MATH-500. Whether the
paper's pessimism extends to prefill DoM is an open empirical
question we plan to settle with P11-FE353 (persistence reprompt),
P11-FE354 (cross-domain AUROC), and P11-FE355 (token-prob residual
AUROC).

**Related experiments:** P11-FE353, P11-FE354, P11-FE355, H-284, H-285,
H-286.

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **Persistence reprompt** — after the model's first answer, send a
  follow-up prompt of the form "Are you sure? Please reconsider." Record
  whether the answer changes. Use change-rate as a behavioral
  confidence proxy.
  *Replication cost*: ~30min H100 for Qwen 1.5B on existing 500
  MATH-500 K=1 greedy problems.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — direct test of refutation #1, gives
  a label-free behavioral confidence signal we can correlate with
  prefill DoM.

- **Self-reported confidence elicitation** — append "On a scale of
  0–100, how confident are you?" to the prompt; parse the integer.
  *Replication cost*: ~30min H100 on the same 500 MATH-500 problems.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — gives a "verbal confidence"
  baseline to contrast with prefill DoM AUROC at problem level. Should
  reveal whether the residual-stream signal captures information not
  present in verbal confidence.

- **Token-level probability vs confidence correlation** — they compute
  the underlying token probability of the model's answer and regress
  self-reported confidence on it. We can do the same with prefill DoM
  score in place of self-reported confidence.
  *Replication cost*: <10min CPU on cached logprobs (we already have
  K=1 greedy generations on H100).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — concrete way to ask "is prefill
  DoM essentially a re-skinning of token-prob, or does it carry
  independent signal?"

### Approaches & framings

- **"Internally coherent sense of confidence" framing.** Decomposes
  confidence into multiple measurable channels (verbal, token-prob,
  reconsideration-stability) and asks whether they cohere. Useful for
  our project: it suggests adding "prefill DoM" as a fourth channel
  and asking whether it coheres with the other three or stands apart
  as a label-required supervised signal. Sharpens H-12's framing —
  label-free coherence is something the paper *denies*.
- **Refutation-by-intervention.** Treats prompted reconsideration as a
  probe of confidence robustness. Analogue for our work: per-position
  DoM steering as a probe of whether the residual-stream confidence
  representation is causal vs correlational (this is exactly P11-FE3,
  but the framing — "intervention-worsens-accuracy is evidence
  *against* a coherent internal signal" — is reusable).

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **BIG-Bench causal-judgment** — ~200 multi-choice causal-reasoning
  questions. HF-available. *Applicable*: yes — primary cross-domain
  test for refutation #2 (does prefill DoM AUROC hold off-MATH-500?).
- **BIG-Bench formal-fallacies** — ~250 logical-fallacy multi-choice
  questions. HF-available. *Applicable*: yes — second cross-domain
  test for refutation #2.
- **Probability/statistical puzzles set** — custom curation by the
  authors; not clearly released as a dataset. *Applicable*: no
  unless they release it; even then, small n and mostly numeric so
  too close to MATH-500 to be a strong cross-domain probe.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- All three evaluated models (GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Mistral) are accessed
  via API or are hosted; the paper does not run open-weights with
  internal-state extraction. Therefore *no* hidden-state activations,
  attention patterns, or residual streams are reported — none of their
  numerical results are directly comparable to our Qwen 1.5B/7B
  L19-based numbers.
- Persistence-prompt format is a single follow-up turn; they do not
  run multi-round Socratic dialogue. Replicating it is a one-extra-call
  experiment.
- They check correlation against token-level probability of the answer
  — implies they have model-supplied logprobs (so Mistral was likely
  run open-weights or via a logprob-returning API). For our pipeline,
  we already have logprobs cached on H100 generations.

### Replicable intermediates

- **Persistence reprompt on Qwen 1.5B MATH-500.** Use cached K=1
  greedy answers from `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute/`. Send
  one extra turn ("Are you sure? Please reconsider.") per problem,
  parse second answer. Compute per-problem persistence flag and
  correlate with prefill DoM score. Direct replication of paper's
  central qualitative-confidence experiment, with the addition of our
  internal-state correlate.
- **Token-prob baseline for prefill DoM.** From cached K=1 generations,
  compute mean log-prob of the answer span per problem (already in
  output JSONs). Train a simple logreg on token-prob alone, compute
  AUROC, compare to F-2's 0.7731 prefill DoM AUROC. Quantifies
  "partially explained by token-prob" for *our* internal signal.
- **Verbal-confidence elicitation on same.** Append confidence question
  to a fresh K=1 pass. Compare verbal-confidence AUROC vs prefill DoM
  AUROC at problem level. Numbers we can run without new GPU time
  (~30min H100 once a pod is up).

### Cross-paper signals

- 2203.11171 — already in graph (status: graphed, REPLICATED+EXTENDED).
  Self-Consistency is the obvious K-budget contrast for the
  reconsideration paradigm; the paper's "second pass worse than first"
  result is the negative-image of self-consistency's "K=many is better
  than K=1" — worth a one-sentence note in PAPER_INDEX.
- 2402.03744 — already in graph (INSIDE / EigenScore, status: CITED ONLY).
  The paper's denial of "internally coherent confidence" is in tension
  with EigenScore's claim that hidden-state covariance carries a clean
  hallucination signal. Worth re-classifying EigenScore's status if
  Pawitan & Holmes' pessimism extends to internal probes.
- 2406.15927 — already in graph (Semantic Entropy Probes, status:
  CITED ONLY). H-12 is the paper-against-paper junction here; this
  brief sharpens the framing.
- Kadavath et al. "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know"
  (2207.05221) — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Closest large-scale
  prior on the same question (LLM self-knowledge calibration), with
  a more optimistic conclusion. Direct counter-evidence to Pawitan &
  Holmes' pessimism — would help bracket the truth.
- Lin et al. "Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words"
  (2205.14334) — already pending_triage in our briefs/ directory; the
  paper directly shows verbal uncertainty *can* be calibrated under
  fine-tuning, which Pawitan & Holmes' off-the-shelf evaluation does
  not contradict.

## 2501.04519 — rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking (Guan, Zhang, Liu, Shang, Sun, Zhu, Yang, Yang — Microsoft Research Asia, 2025)

**Relevance:** Same model family (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B, Phi3-mini), same primary benchmark (MATH-500) as our P11 H100 baseline. Directly addresses our H-19 (C_exact verification beats C_infer scaling at matched compute) with the strongest existence proof to date: 7B+PPM beats 72B+ORM Best-of-N. Their PPM training methodology (Bradley-Terry on Q-value-derived preference pairs) is a direct alternative framing to our F-2 (single-direction prefill DoM) — and we can test it on cached activations without MCTS.

**Key claim we tested:** A step-level process preference model (PPM) with Bradley-Terry loss on Q-value-derived pairs is the dominant performance lever in System-2 math reasoning, not the policy model — once policy capability is "reasonable."

**Our result:** **TO TEST.** No experiments run yet. Two cheap follow-ups (FE73 Q-value correlation, FE74 step-boundary probe) directly test rStar-Math's PPM framing against F-2 on our cached data without requiring their model. FE75 (D-bucket under rStar-Math) is BLOCKED on weight release.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE356, P11-FE357, P11-FE358, P11-FE359, P11-FE360, H-287, H-288, H-289, EXP-040 (D-bucket original characterization), H-19.

**Status:** TO TEST (HIGH priority — H-287 and H-288 are CPU-only and directly bound F-2's "best signal" claim).

### Methodologies extracted

- **MCTS with code-augmented CoT** — each candidate step generates Python code; only successfully executing code is retained as a valid node, then UCT selects best of n.
  *Replication cost:* Medium. We have Qwen2.5-Math-7B activations cached but no MCTS infrastructure. ~1 week H100 to set up step-level rollouts + code execution sandbox.
  *We'd plausibly run this:* No — too expensive relative to its diagnostic value for our F-N findings. We'd run it only if a partner releases the rStar-Math weights and inference code (https://github.com/microsoft/rStar).

- **Process Preference Model (PPM) via Bradley-Terry pairwise loss** — for each step, top-2 Q-value steps as positive, bottom-2 as negative, train scalar head with `−log σ(r_θ(x, y_pos) − r_θ(x, y_neg))`. Crucially, positives must lead to a correct final answer and negatives to incorrect.
  *Replication cost:* Low. ~4h CPU + small GPU once we have step-segmented K=8 trajectories with outcomes (we already have K=8 outcome labels; we'd need step boundary parsing and a probe head training script).
  *We'd plausibly run this:* Yes — directly tests Refutation #2 against F-2.

- **Q-value back-propagation** — terminal node q∈{−1, +1}, q(s_i)^k = q(s_i)^(k−1) + q(s_d)^k; provides intermediate-step labels without human annotation.
  *Replication cost:* Trivial scripting on cached K=8 outcome data. ~2h CPU.
  *We'd plausibly run this:* Yes — generates intermediate-step Q-labels for our existing K=8 trajectories, useful for H-5 (does prefill-DoM correlate with mean-Q) and H-19 (does layer-wise probe at step boundaries beat prefill).

- **PPM-augmented MCTS rollout for hard problems** — start with 16 rollouts, escalate to 64 then 128 with new random seeds for unsolved problems.
  *Replication cost:* High; requires their full pipeline.
  *We'd plausibly run this:* No, except via their released artifacts.

- **Self-evolution loop** — round k: policy_k + PPM_k → MCTS data → SFT policy_{k+1}, train PPM_{k+1}; 4 rounds.
  *Replication cost:* Very high (~$5–10k compute, weeks).
  *We'd plausibly run this:* No.

### Approaches & framings

- **System 2 reasoning as MCTS over step-CoT-with-code** — recasts test-time compute allocation as tree search over verifiable atomic steps rather than full-solution Best-of-N. Intersects our H-19 (C_exact vs C_infer): rStar-Math is C_exact maximally pushed.
- **"PPM shapes the reasoning boundary"** — claim that once policy capability is "reasonable," the reward model is the binding constraint on System-2 performance. Reframes our prefill-DoM question: if PPM is the binding constraint and prefill-DoM is a cheap PPM proxy, then F-2's value lies upstream of policy quality.
- **Q-values as preference labels, not score labels** — rejects the implicit assumption that step-level reward must be a calibrated scalar. Suggests our F-2 framing ("DoM as a calibrated AUROC") is sub-optimal for downstream selection vs PPM-style ranking.
- **Step-by-step verification as data filter, not just inference** — validates the "intermediate-step probing" agenda our H-13 (head-level attribution of prefill vs final-token circuits) sits in.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **MATH-500** — 500 problems, Hendrycks et al. license, HF accessible. **Applicable: yes** — already our canonical benchmark.
- **AIME 2024** — 30 problems, HF (`AI-MO/aimo-validation-aime`), public. **Applicable: yes** for cross-difficulty test of H-5 (familiarity vs decomposability) — these are unfamiliar competition problems.
- **AMC 2023** — ~83 problems, HF (`AI-MO/aimo-validation-amc`). **Applicable: yes**, similar use as AIME.
- **Olympiad Bench** — 8,476 problems (text-only math subset commonly used), HF. **Applicable: yes**, but heavy — only valuable if we're willing to run 1024-tok extraction at scale.
- **College Math** — Tang et al. 2024, ~2.8k problems, HF. **Applicable: yes** for cross-domain prefill-DoM transfer (extension of P5 cross-benchmark).
- **GaokaoEn 2023** — Liao et al. 2024, ~358 problems. **Applicable: marginal** — Chinese-origin, language confound for our Qwen evaluation.
- **rStar-Math 747k training set (NuminaMath + MetaMath + GPT-4 synthetic)** — license mixed, partially gated. **Applicable: no** — training-set-scale, not a benchmark.
- **rStar-Math step-by-step verified trajectories** (claimed release at https://github.com/microsoft/rStar). **Applicable: yes if released** — would enable "score our prefill DoM against their Q-values" cross-check at zero MCTS cost.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- Code: https://github.com/microsoft/rStar (claimed; verify).
- Bradley-Terry pairwise loss for PPM (Eq. 4): `L_ppm = −E_{(x,y_pos,y_neg)} log σ(r_θ(x,y_pos) − r_θ(x,y_neg))`.
- PPM head: linear + tanh → output in [−1, 1].
- UCT exploration constant `c` (unspecified in the snippet; standard √2 likely).
- 4 rounds, 16 rollouts/problem normally, 64–128 for hard Olympiad-level.
- Code execution as filter — Python-execution pass required for a step to be a valid MCTS child.
- Round-1 bootstrap uses DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct (236B) as policy because the 7B SLM can't generate good initial solutions; rounds 2–4 use the fine-tuned 7B SLM.
- Hardware: 4 × 40GB A100 for MCTS rollouts (claimed accessible).
- Final answer step relaxes the same-prefix preference-pair constraint (positive-trajectory mean-Q vs negative-trajectory mean-Q).
- Q-values are bounded in [−1, +1] by construction, so the tanh head is calibration-friendly.

### Replicable intermediates

- **Q-value labels for our existing K=8 MATH-500 trajectories** — apply Eq. 2 to our cached K=8 outcomes from `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute/results.json`. Even without MCTS, we can compute back-propagated Q-values along each K=8 trajectory using a coarse step-segmentation (e.g., NL-newline boundaries). ~2h CPU. Lets us test correlation between prefill DoM percentile and mean-Q (H-5 direct test).
- **Step-boundary probe at L19** — for each K=8 trajectory in our cache, segment by `\n\n` step delimiters, extract L19 mean-pooled activations per step, train a Bradley-Terry head against (top-2-Q, bottom-2-Q) pairs. Compare to F-2's 0.7731 prefill AUROC. ~4h CPU on cached activations. Direct test of Refutation #2.
- **D-bucket evaluation under MCTS** — *not* fully replicable from our cache; requires their model. Track release of microsoft/rStar.
- **Length-vs-PPM-gain bucket** — Re-stratify rStar-Math's reported MATH-500 numbers by trajectory length (when they release per-problem outputs); test Refutation #4 mechanism.
- **Cross-domain transfer of prefill DoM to AIME/AMC** — our existing 1.5B prefill DoM extractor against AIME 2024 (30 problems) and AMC 2023 (~83 problems). H100 day. Tests whether F-2 generalizes beyond MATH.

### Cross-paper signals

- **2203.11171** — already in graph (status: graphed). Self-Consistency K-sample voting is one of rStar-Math's named baselines (Wang et al. 2023).
- **2410.13640** — likely cited (CoE / Wang et al.); already in graph (PARTIALLY CONFIRMED). Both papers do step-level analysis but rStar-Math reaches different conclusion on whether per-step trajectory features are needed.
- **2305.20050** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Lightman et al. "Let's Verify Step-by-Step" (PRM800k) — the canonical PRM citation rStar-Math contrasts itself against. Direct grandparent paper for any process-reward discussion in our research-graph.
- **2408.03314** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Snell et al. "Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally" — the canonical compute-scaling reference for H-19. Likely the strongest single predictor of H-19's mechanism.
- **2406.06592** — NOT in graph; possibly worth admission. Wang et al. 2024c (math-shepherd / process-reward via MCTS) — direct prior method that rStar-Math's PPM improves on.
- **2403.04706** — NOT in graph; possible admission for H-19 context.
- **2310.01798** — NOT in graph; Huang et al. self-correction critique — bears on rStar-Math's self-reflection finding (which we should treat skeptically).

## 2501.11036 — LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models (Yang, Li, Wang, Zhou, Feng, Peng, 2025)

**Relevance:** LF-Steering compares activation steering at three granularities (raw hidden-state direction = ActAdd/CAA; attention-head outputs = ITI/SCS; SAE-disentangled feature level = LF-Steering) and shows feature-level dominates by ≥4–9% accuracy and has tighter locality/OOD-neutrality on Llama2-7B. Our entire P10/P11 steering thread (H-1, EXP-037-style raw DoM injection) sits at the *worst* of those three granularities by their analysis. The paper does not study correctness on MATH-500, but its polysemanticity argument is directly applicable to L19 DoM and motivates a feature-level reformulation of F-2 and H-1.

**Key claim we tested:** "Raw layer-wide hidden-state directions (ActAdd/CAA, by extension our L19 DoM) are polysemanticity-limited; SAE-disentangled feature-level steering substantially outperforms direction-level steering with better locality."

**Our result:** **TO TEST** Their claim is novel, narrowly-scoped to NLU/NLG semantic consistency on Llama2-7B-Chat, and does not test correctness on a multi-step reasoning benchmark. We have cached Qwen-2.5-1.5B L19 activations on MATH-500 ready, and the LF-Steering recipe transports cleanly. P11-FE361 (probe AUROC) and P11-FE362 (steering accuracy delta) directly test whether F-2 and H-1 are polysemanticity-ceiling-limited.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE361, P11-FE362, P11-FE363, H-290, H-291, H-1 (dependent reframing).

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **TopK SAE pretraining (Gao et al. 2024 method, applied here)** — train a TopK sparse autoencoder mapping 4096-dim hidden states → 65,536-dim feature space, k=192 retained, on 850K open-domain RedPajama subset, 32K steps, lr 2e-4. *Replication cost*: H100-week for Qwen-1.5B/7B from scratch; **hours** if a pre-trained Qwen SAE (e.g., Goodfire's Ember or community SAE-lens checkpoints) can be reused. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — but only via a pre-trained checkpoint; from-scratch SAE training is out-of-budget for a single triage refutation.
- **Top-1 transformer layer locating via per-layer classifier (Yang et al. 2024)** — for each layer, train a binary classifier on concatenated `[h(m), h(n)]` from semantically-equivalent prompt pairs `(m, n)` with consistency label `l`; pick layer with highest test accuracy. *Replication cost*: 30min CPU on cached activations. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — as a methodological alternative to our PR-by-layer / DoM-AUROC-by-layer search; cheap sanity check that L19 is the right layer for *correctness* under this classifier-driven definition of "the right layer."
- **Key feature locating via average feature difference + threshold** — feed (correct, rephrased-incorrect) contrastive pairs `(u, v)` through pretrained SAE, take last-token features `z(u), z(v)`, compute mean `|z(u) - z(v)|` over the 500-pair dataset, threshold at `t = 0.10` to get key feature index set `I`. *Replication cost*: 1h CPU on cached activations + a Qwen SAE checkpoint. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — this is the smallest concrete cross-check for Refutation 3.
- **Feature-level activation steering at inference** — encode hidden state through SAE, for each `i ∈ I` with `z_i(q) ≠ 0`, set `z_i(q) ← z_i(q) + α · g_i` where `g_i` is the per-feature average difference, decode back through SAE decoder, replace the layer's hidden state. `α = 20`. *Replication cost*: H100-day for full MATH-500 sweep. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly competes with H-1's raw DoM steering; would strengthen H-1 to "DoM steering on disentangled features moves MATH-500 accuracy."
- **Out-of-domain locality testing** — measure whether steering hurts unrelated tasks (AG News, IMDB, CNN/Daily Mail, XSum). LF-Steering shows their method is OOD-neutral while ActAdd hurts AG News by 2.8 points. *Replication cost*: 2h H100. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — required regularizer for any H-1 "DoM steering moves accuracy" claim; without it we cannot rule out cross-domain damage.
- **Hyperparameter sweep on `t` and `α`** — `t ∈ {0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30}`, `α ∈ {5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50}`. They report peak at `t=0.10, α=20`, with extreme α=50 degrading. *Replication cost*: included in the sweep above. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — informs our H-1 α range, which is currently `{-4,-2,-1,0,1,2,4}` and may be 5–10× too small.

### Approaches & framings

- **Polysemanticity as the explanation for raw-direction probes' ceiling.** Reframes our F-2 as "single L19 direction is the best *single direction*, not the best L19 signal." Useful as a counterfactual frame for narrative writeup and for any future P11 ceiling discussion.
- **"Grey-box" vs "black-box" steering taxonomy.** Useful framing language if Pathway 11 is ever written up as a paper — situates DoM probing/steering as a grey-box, in contrast to SFT-based correctness alignment.
- **Coarse-to-fine localization** (layer-first → feature-within-layer). Cleanly nests with our pathway-by-layer investigation; if SAE features are tractable for Qwen, "feature-within-L19" becomes a natural P11 sub-pathway.
- **Locality (OOD-neutrality) as a steering-method regularizer.** The paper makes a strong case that locality should be reported alongside any steering result. Recommends a tightening of H-1's success criterion from "moves MATH-500 accuracy" to "moves MATH-500 accuracy with bounded OOD degradation" before any steering claim is promoted to F-status.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **RobustBOOLQ** — 500 samples, paraphrase-augmented BoolQ. License: derived from BoolQ (CC). Accessibility: gated/scrape-from-Yang-2024. Applicable? no — NLU consistency, not MATH correctness.
- **RobustSST2** — 500 samples, paraphrase-augmented SST2. License: SST2 (open). Applicable? no — sentiment NLU.
- **RobustMRPC** — 500 samples, paraphrase-augmented MRPC. License: MRPC (open). Applicable? no — paraphrase NLU.
- **PopQA Sport / PopQA Capital** — NLG factoid QA with paraphrased prompts. Accessibility: derived from PopQA (HF). Applicable? no — factoid QA, not multi-step reasoning.
- **AG News, IMDB** — locality-test NLU classification, 500 samples each. License: open. Applicable? **yes, weakly** — could serve as a fast OOD locality probe for any DoM-steering experiment we run on Qwen-1.5B (test that steering correctness on MATH doesn't tank AG News classification accuracy).
- **CNN/Daily Mail, XSum** — locality-test NLG summarization, 500 samples each, ROUGE-L scoring. License: open. Applicable? **yes, weakly** — same role as above for NLG-side locality.
- **RedPajama-Data-1T-Sample (850K subset)** — SAE pretraining corpus. License: HF, open. Applicable? yes — if we ever train a Qwen SAE from scratch.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- TopK SAE: 4096→65536, k=192. RedPajama 850K subset, 32K steps, lr 2e-4, batch 1/GPU on 8×V100 32GB. Total ≈4 GPU-days.
- Steering hyperparameters: feature-difference threshold `t = 0.10`, steering strength `α = 20`. α range tested: [5, 50], peak at 20, degrades by α=50.
- Layer-locating dataset: 500 (m, n, l) instances from Yang et al. 2024, 4:1 train:test split. Per-layer linear classifier on concatenated hidden states.
- Key feature locator: `g_i = (1/|D_f|) Σ |z_i(u) - z_i(v)|`, `I = {i : g_i > t}`. Steering bias `b_i = g_i` for `i ∈ I` and `z_i(q) ≠ 0`.
- Feature interpretation done manually post-hoc on top-ranked feature IDs (Table 2).
- No code link in the paper. SCS baseline code: github.com/nrimsky/CAA references, but LF-Steering itself has no public repo flagged in the manuscript.

### Replicable intermediates

- **Method-A (cheap, single-day):** load a publicly-released Qwen-2.5-1.5B SAE (Goodfire-Ember or SAE-lens hub if available for L19); encode the cached `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute` L19 prefill activations for the 500 MATH-500 problems; compute `g_i` over (correct=243, incorrect=257) pairs (sampling 250 random pairs); threshold `t=0.10`; report (a) `|I|` size, (b) sparse-feature logistic probe AUROC vs F-2's 0.7731, (c) cosine of feature-mass-vector at prefill vs final-token positions for Refutation 2.
- **Method-B (no-SAE fallback):** PCA the L19 prefill activations into 50 components, fit per-component logistic probes, take the top-K by AUROC, ensemble. This is *not* SAE but it tests whether the polysemanticity story is at least directionally correct (more-than-1-direction probes should beat single DoM direction). 1h CPU on cached NPZs.
- **Method-C (locality-only):** Run our existing DoM steering plan (H-1) on AG News and IMDB 500-sample subsets with the same α as MATH-500; report whether AG News / IMDB accuracy degrades. 2h H100.

If no Qwen-1.5B SAE is publicly available, Method-A is gated on a Goodfire/SAE-lens checkpoint search (~1h reconnaissance).

### Cross-paper signals

- **2306.03341** — already in graph (status: graphed). ITI / inference-time intervention. LF-Steering's SCS baseline lineage; relevant for any feature-vs-head comparison.
- **2308.10248** — already in graph (status: pending_triage, admission_only brief). ActAdd. LF-Steering's weakest baseline; documented to *hurt* AG News locality, useful corroboration for "raw-direction steering is fragile."
- **2406.04093** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Gao et al. "Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders" (TopK SAE method paper). Direct dependency for any feature-level steering replication.
- **2403.19647** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Marks et al. "Sparse Feature Circuits." LF-Steering's explicit future-work pointer for multi-layer feature steering; directly relevant to Refutation 4 (multi-layer feature circuits).
- **2309.08600** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Cunningham et al. "Sparse autoencoders find highly interpretable features in language models" — foundational SAE-as-interpretability paper.
- **2209.10652** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Elhage et al. "Toy Models of Superposition." Theoretical underpinning of polysemanticity; cited as the framing for why raw-direction probes leave signal on the table.
- **2404.16014** — NOT in graph; not yet recommend (lower priority). Rajamanoharan et al. "Improving dictionary learning with gated sparse autoencoders." Gated-SAE alternative; only matters if we end up training SAEs from scratch.

## 2501.12934 — Correctness Assessment of Code Generated by Large Language Models Using Internal Representations (OPENIA) (Bui, Vu, Nguyen, Nguyen, Vo, 2025)

**Relevance:** Trains a 2-hidden-layer MLP probe on hidden states of code LLMs (DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B/6.7B, CodeLlama 7B/13B, Magicoder 7B) to predict whether generated code passes its tests. Reports cross-task accuracy 0.73–0.79 across HumanEval / MBPP / DevEval, beating CodeBERT / CodeT5+ post-hoc classifiers and LLM-Check by up to 40 %. The headline configuration uses **last code token at last layer**; layer-sweep places the optimum in the middle-to-late layers (L16–L28 across architectures). This is the exact methodology family our F-2 / F-3 / F-8 / H-3 sit in, applied to the code-generation domain.

**Key claim we tested (in our terms):** A non-linear single-token probe over a single mid-to-late layer of a code-LLM hidden state encodes binary correctness with weighted-F1 ≥ 0.73 cross-task / ≥ 0.86 repo-level, and the *last-token-at-last-layer* is the canonical readout — contradicting our F-2 ordering of prefill > final-token. The paper also reports stability of probe performance across token positions at deep layers, which contradicts F-3's near-orthogonality of prefill and final DoM.

**Our result:** **TO TEST.** The paper's last-token / last-layer probe has not been reproduced on Qwen-2.5-1.5B MATH-500 yet. P11-FE364 (replicate on Qwen) and P11-FE365 (token-invariance scan) are the two head-to-head experiments that decide whether F-2 / F-3 generalize across domain or are math-CoT-specific. Until those run, the paper sits in TO TEST as a *high-leverage refutation candidate*.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE364, P11-FE365, P11-FE366, P11-FE367, P11-FE368; H-292, H-293, H-294, H-295; bears on F-2, F-3, F-8, F-9, H-3, H-11.

**Status:** TO TEST (HIGH priority — the refutation chain to F-2 / F-3 is direct and the cost of the cross-checks is < 2 hours of CPU on cached NPZs).

### Methodologies extracted

- **2-hidden-layer MLP probe over single-token hidden state** — fully-connected 128/64 head, 50 epochs, batch 32, lr 1e-3, weighted-F1 objective. *Replication cost*: ~1 minute on a small GPU per probe. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — drop-in alternative to our linear DoM probe to test whether non-linearity in the probe head moves AUROC on Qwen-2.5-1.5B.
- **Last-code-token at last layer probing** — extract `h_{L,m}` where `c_m` is the last token of the generated code segment (skipping any post-code natural-language tokens). *Replication cost*: 20min CPU on cached NPZs. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly tests refutation #1 on MATH-500.
- **Per-layer probe sweep with selection** — fit probe at every layer, report best. *Replication cost*: 30min CPU on cached `pathway11_h100/layerwise_dom`. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — already partially done; reframe through "stability across tokens at that layer" lens.
- **Per-token-position probe sweep** — fit probe at fixed depth across {first token, last token, first code token, last code token}. *Replication cost*: 1h CPU. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly tests refutation #2 (token invariance at deep layers).
- **CG² (Correctness-Guided Generation)** — best-of-K decoding with probe-score-weighted selection. *Replication cost*: 20min CPU on cached K=8 MATH-500 samples (we already have multi-sample data via Pathway 11). *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — direct comparator for F-8 selective-prediction.
- **Probe-as-LLM-benchmark** — Pearson correlation between probe-predicted-correct rate and pass@1 across models (their values: 0.99 / 0.73 / 0.97). *Replication cost*: 10min once per-model probes exist. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — sanity check on whether DoM-predicted accuracy tracks measured K=1 accuracy across Qwen-2.5-1.5B / 7B.
- **Cross-language generalization split** — train on N-1 languages, test on Nth. *Replication cost*: not directly applicable (we're math-only). *We'd plausibly run this*: no — no MATH multi-language analogue.
- **LLM-as-A-Judge (LLM-AJ) baseline** — both in-house and external (o4-mini) zero-shot prompted correctness judgment. *Replication cost*: o4-mini API budget ~ $20 for MATH-500. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — useful black-box ceiling for our F-8 numbers and H-12.
- **LLM-Check baseline** — Eigen-analysis of hidden states + attention-map kernels + token-level uncertainty. *Replication cost*: medium (paper [40] code). *We'd plausibly run this*: maybe — overlaps with EigenScore (PAPER_INDEX 2402.03744) and EigenTrack. Worth admitting LLM-Check to the graph if we ever write up Pathway 11 breathing.
- **Length-binning of probe F1** — bin generated outputs by token-length, report F1 per bin. *Replication cost*: 10min CPU. *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — analogous to H-15 length-band PR control.

### Approaches & framings

- **"Open-box / white-box" framing for reliability assessment** — argues code-LLMs are uniquely tractable for in-process correctness probing because every intermediate state is accessible and ground-truth correctness is *objectively decidable* via tests. Intersects our F-8 / H-12: if MATH-500 numerical-correctness is similarly decidable (which it is), our results sit in the same epistemic bucket as OPENIA's, not the noisier NLG-hallucination literature. Useful framing in any writeup.
- **Process-oriented vs output-oriented probing** — OPENIA distinguishes "probing internal states during generation" (process) from "probing the final output" (post-hoc). Maps onto our prefill-vs-final-token decomposition (F-2, F-3) but assigns different semantics: prefill ≈ "model's pre-decoding state" rather than "process-during-generation."
- **Last-code-token as universal terminal aggregator** — claim that the *last token of the generated code* (not last token of the full response) is the canonical readout. We have not separated "answer-region terminal" from "post-answer-newline" (PANL) in our analysis (cf. H-18). This is a token-selection refinement F-2 may have missed.
- **Layer-architecture conditional probe selection** — argues against fixing a single layer index; advocates per-model dynamic layer choice. Bears on our cross-scale stitching plans (H-11) and any future cross-architecture replication.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **HumanEval** — 164 standalone Python tasks; HF accessible; canonical code benchmark. *Applicable?* yes — directly tests H-3 if we run Qwen-2.5-Coder or DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B on it with our hidden-state pipeline.
- **MBPP** — 500 standalone Python tasks; HF accessible. *Applicable?* yes — same as HumanEval, for cross-task / cross-benchmark splits.
- **DevEval** — 1,825 manually-annotated repo-level Python tasks; HF accessible; tests context-dependent generation. *Applicable?* yes, but heavy — only if H-3 needs the repo-level stress test.
- **HumanEval multi-language** — Python / JS / TS / Java / C++ / C# / PHP / Bash. *Applicable?* no (we're math-domain).
- **OPENIA dataset** (24,890 generated code units + extracted hidden states) — released at https://github.com/iSE-UET-VNU/OPENIA. *Applicable?* yes — gives us a free off-the-shelf code-domain comparison set without needing 86 hours of A6000 extraction.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- Code: https://github.com/iSE-UET-VNU/OPENIA
- DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B: 32 transformer layers, 4096 hidden dim. Best-layer = 20 (independent-unit) / 28 (repo-level).
- CodeLlama-7B: 32 layers. Best-layer = 16 (independent-unit) / 32 (repo-level).
- Magicoder-7B: 32 layers. Best-layer = 28 (both settings).
- Probe: input → 128 → 64 → 2-class softmax; 50 epochs, batch 32, lr 1e-3.
- 10 candidate solutions per task generated for training data.
- Inference: 0.6 ms per code unit on P100; total probe-training ~1 min.
- Hidden-state extraction: 86 hours on NVIDIA A6000 48 GB for 24,890 units.
- Cross-benchmark MBPP→HumanEval is **prompt-template-sensitive**: F1 drops 0.79→0.67 on DeepSeek-6.7B due to wording differences. Mitigated to 0.72 via mixed-prompt training.
- Code-length effect: F1 = 0.81 for 1–30 tok, dips to 0.66 at 51–70 tok, recovers >70 tok.
- Difficulty effect: U-shape — easy (0.75 F1) and hard (high) > medium-difficulty.

### Replicable intermediates

- **Last-token-last-layer probe on Qwen-2.5-1.5B MATH-500** (refutation #1 test): use `pathway11_h100/` cached NPZ for hidden states; need last-decoded-token at last layer L27. If layer 27 isn't cached, fall back to last cached layer. Train MLP 128/64. Compare AUROC vs F-2's 0.7731.
- **Token-invariance scan** (refutation #2 test): cached `pathway11_h100/layerwise_dom` likely has per-layer first-token and final-token DoM. Compute cos per layer; produce a curve. ~20min CPU.
- **CG² on cached K=8 MATH-500 samples**: if `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute` has per-sample probe scores, sort and pick the top-1. Compare to plain K=1 accuracy 48.6 %. ~10min.
- **LLM-AJ in-house baseline** on MATH-500: prompt Qwen-2.5-1.5B / 7B with "is the following math solution correct?" zero-shot. ~30min on H100 (or local CPU at low TPS).
- **Probe-pass@1 Pearson** (sanity check): correlate per-problem prefill_DoM predicted-correct rate with measured pass@1 across our two models. ~5min on cached JSONs.

### Cross-paper signals

- **2402.03744** — INSIDE / EigenScore (Chen et al., ICLR 2024). Already in graph (CITED ONLY). OPENIA cites it as ref [39] and benchmarks its INSIDE-derivative LLM-Check (ref [40]) against. Connection: another internal-state probe that targets NLG hallucination.
- **2306.03341** — Inference-Time Intervention (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023). Already in graph (CONTRADICTED). OPENIA cites as ref [102]. Same conceptual lineage of probing-then-steering.
- **2406.12541** (LLM-Check, Sriramanan et al., NeurIPS 2024) — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Uses Eigen-analysis of hidden states + attention map kernels + token-level uncertainty as a *training-free* hallucination detector. Direct conceptual sibling of EigenScore (already in graph) and a methodological alternative to our DoM probe. Worth admitting because it gives a parameter-free baseline for F-2/F-8.
- **2306.13063** (Azaria & Mitchell, EMNLP 2023, "The internal state of an LLM knows when it's lying") — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Earliest hidden-state-truthfulness probe; foundational citation for any prefill / mid-generation correctness story (F-2, H-12).
- **2406.12673** (Gottesman & Geva, "Estimating knowledge in LLMs without generating a single token") — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Argues that *first-prompt-token* hidden states alone encode answer correctness — a stronger version of our F-2 prefill claim. Highly relevant to F-2 lineage.

## 2501.12948 — DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning (DeepSeek-AI, 2025)

**Relevance:** R1 is the canonical reasoning-RL paper of 2025 and the
direct upstream of `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B`, an
architecturally drop-in replacement for the project's base
Qwen-2.5-1.5B. The paper's claims about emergent reflection ("aha
moment", §2.3) and outcome-only RL with rule-based reward provide the
single sharpest test we have of whether F-2 (prefill AUROC), F-3
(prefill ⊥ final), and F-1 (universal breathing) survive aggressive
post-training that adds long CoT and self-revision. It also frames our
selective-prediction work (F-8, H-19) inside a broader "dynamic compute
allocation" research program.

**Key claim we tested:** Reasoning capability can be incentivized in
LLMs via outcome-only RL with rule-based reward (no SFT prelude, no
process reward), and the resulting model exhibits emergent reflection
visible as a sharp behavioral discontinuity at training step 8.2k.
Distilling these reasoning trajectories into Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B yields
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, which has the same architecture as our
project's base model.

**Our result:** **TO TEST** — none of the headline replicable
intermediates (P11-FE369/71/72/73, H-296/73/74) have been run yet.
Distillation is not directly relevant to the project's findings, but
the released R1-distill checkpoint is the most actionable lever for
testing F-1, F-2, F-3, F-8, F-9 generalization across post-training
conditions. The "aha moment" anthropomorphism in §2.3 should be read
through the Ríos-García (2604.18805) frame.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE369, P10-FE20, P11-FE370, P11-FE371,
P11-FE372, H-296, H-297, H-298

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)** — PPO without a value model;
  advantage = (r_i − group_mean) / group_std over G samples per question.
  *Replication cost*: $50K+ H100 for full training; trivial in TRL/verl
  for toy validation.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no — out of scope; but worth knowing the
  reference policy is swapped every 400 steps, which is an experimental
  knob other papers don't expose.

- **Outcome-only rule-based reward (no PRM, no ORM, no neural RM)** —
  accuracy reward (sympy / compiler / option matching) + format reward
  (`<think>...</think><answer>...</answer>`) + language reward.
  *Replication cost*: minimal; the design lesson is the explicit refusal
  to use neural reward models for reasoning ("susceptible to reward
  hacking during large-scale RL").
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no — but it informs how we should treat
  any neural-RM-derived correctness label in our own datasets.

- **Reflection / "aha-moment" detector** — the paper tracks frequency of
  the word "wait" during CoT generation (Figure 9b in their supplement)
  and shows a sharp jump at step 8.2k.
  *Replication cost*: 30min CPU on existing P11 generations.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — running this on our cached MATH-500
  generations from base Qwen-2.5-1.5B vs R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B would tell
  us whether reflection events are present in our regime, which gates
  refutations 3 and 5.

- **Long-CoT context expansion (32k → 65k tokens at step 8.2k)** —
  curriculum-style increase of max generation length partway through RL.
  *Replication cost*: needs RL infrastructure we don't run.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no — but informs interpretation of our
  1024-tok labelling regime as drastically truncated relative to R1.

- **Cold-start SFT + 2-stage RL (rejection-sampling SFT between stages)** —
  thousands of human-readable seed traces → first RL → rejection-sample
  600k correct traces → SFT → second RL (mixed reasoning + preference).
  *Replication cost*: O(GPU-month) per stage at any meaningful size.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no.

- **DeepSeek-V3-as-judge for non-rule-verifiable rewards (Listing 4)** —
  generative LLM-judge prompt with explicit "correct/incorrect" output
  field for cases where sympy/compiler can't decide.
  *Replication cost*: API cost only.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes for a small bucket — could replace our
  current correctness labelling on edge cases where extractor sympy
  parsing fails.

- **Language consistency reward (proportion of target-language tokens in
  CoT)** — added to total reward, slightly degrades benchmark accuracy
  but improves readability.
  *Replication cost*: trivial.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no — not in scope.

- **High GRPO clip ratio ε = 10** — the paper notes (§3.2.1) "clip ratio
  plays a crucial role; lower values truncate gradients for many tokens,
  higher values cause instability." 10 is dramatically larger than the
  standard 0.2 used in PPO/GRPO literature.
  *Replication cost*: hyperparameter for any future RL fine-tune.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: only if H-1 graduates to a real RL steering
  experiment (currently parked).

### Approaches & framings

- **"Pure RL beats SFT for reasoning"** — direct challenge to the framing
  that human reasoning trajectories are upper-bound supervisors. F-2's
  AUROC measurement implicitly assumes the model arrives at correctness
  via an SFT-style trajectory; if R1 is right, our prefill probe
  measures something specific to that trajectory class.

- **"Reasoning capability is *incentivized*, not designed"** — the paper
  argues reasoning circuits already exist in the base model; RL just
  amplifies them. This is the conjugate of H-1's framing (DoM is a
  steering signal we can inject) — the alternative framing is that GRPO
  has *already* sculpted the same direction we're trying to find with
  probing.

- **"Token efficiency = dynamic compute allocation"** (their §6 limitation
  framing). They explicitly position their model against majority voting
  and MCTS, claiming dynamic allocation is intrinsically more efficient.
  This is the same dichotomy we have between C_infer (sample more) and
  C_exact (think harder per sample) — H-19.

- **"Reward hacking is the bottleneck for general RL"** — neural reward
  models break under large-scale RL. This is a methodological warning for
  any future probing-as-reward work (H-1 v2 if anyone proposed RL'ing the
  L19 DoM as an objective).

- **Distillation > small-model RL** — Supplementary F (not loaded here
  because the HF rendering omits the distillation table) reportedly
  shows that SFT'ing R1 reasoning traces into Qwen-2.5-1.5B beats running
  GRPO on Qwen-2.5-1.5B directly. This re-frames "small-model reasoning"
  as a data problem, not a training-algorithm problem.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **AIME 2024** — 30 problems, math olympiad. Public, accessible. Applicable?
  yes — short-answer numeric, fits our extractor pipeline. Different
  difficulty regime from MATH-500 (R1-Zero: 77.9% AIME pass@1 vs 95.9%
  MATH-500 pass@1).
- **MATH-500** — already our canonical benchmark. R1: 97.3%. Applicable?
  trivially.
- **GPQA Diamond** — graduate-level science multiple-choice; HF-accessible.
  Applicable? yes — for testing F-2 outside math.
- **CNMO 2024** — Chinese National High School Math Olympiad. Applicable?
  yes if we want a Chinese-language test of breathing universality (F-1).
- **LiveCodeBench (2024-08 to 2025-01)** — coding benchmark, time-windowed
  to avoid contamination. HF. Applicable? yes for H-3 (breathing on code).
- **Codeforces / Aider-Polyglot / SWE-Bench Verified** — engineering
  benchmarks; non-trivial scoring infrastructure. Applicable? yes for
  H-3, but heavier lift.
- **800k SFT distillation data** — not released as far as I can tell.
  Applicable? no — but the *distilled models trained on it are released*
  on HF (`deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B` etc).
- **26K RL math prompts / 17K code / 22K STEM / 15K logic / 66K general** —
  not released. Applicable? no.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- **R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B** is on HF (`deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B`),
  same architecture as our current Qwen-2.5-1.5B (28 layers, 1536 hidden) —
  drop-in for our P11 extractor with no code changes. **This is the single
  most actionable lever from this paper.**
- **R1-Distill-Qwen-7B** is similarly drop-in for the 7B extractor.
- Long-CoT default temperature 1.0 during rollout (we run 0 / greedy);
  lower temperature 0.7 in the second RL stage; "few-shot prompting
  consistently degrades performance" — they recommend zero-shot.
- Maximum context they use during eval is 65,536 tokens; our 1024-tok
  labelling regime is therefore ~64× shorter than R1's natural inference
  envelope. Direct comparison numbers are not apples-to-apples.
- GRPO hyperparameters they used: lr=3e-6, KL coef=0.001, ε_clip=10,
  G=16 group size, batch=512, ref policy refresh every 400 steps,
  10,400 total steps = 1.6 epochs.
- Code repo: https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1
- Author list at end shows Zhibin Gou led the R1-Distill series — useful
  if we ever email them.

### Replicable intermediates

- **Run frozen P11 prefill+L19+DoM extractor on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B for
  50 MATH-500 problems** — gives a fast read on whether F-2 AUROC

  Refutes/confirms F-3 in one number.
- **"Wait" token frequency on our cached MATH-500 generations** — 30 min
  CPU regex sweep over our existing K=1 generations from base
  Qwen-2.5-1.5B vs Qwen-2.5-7B, separated by correct/incorrect. Cheap
  test of whether reflection-style language is even present in our
  regime.
- **Peak PR comparison: base Qwen-2.5-1.5B vs R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on
  matched 50-prompt subset** — directly tests F-1 universality vs H-10
  (post-training shifts). H100 hours for R1-distill activations + CPU

## 2502.01126 — Language Models Prefer What They Know: Relative Confidence Estimation via Confidence Preferences (Shrivastava, Kumar, Liang, 2025)

**Relevance:** Direct competitor to F-2 / F-8 as a *label-free, internals-free* correctness predictor. The paper introduces pairwise relative-confidence elicitation aggregated by Elo / TrueSkill / Bradley-Terry and reports an average AUROC of 0.753 across 5 frontier closed/open models on 14 QA datasets — the same order of magnitude as our F-2 prefill L19 DoM AUROC of 0.7731 on Qwen-1.5B / MATH-500. They also report a striking *difficulty-only* result (GPT-4o AUC 0.819 without seeing its own answers, vs 0.872 with), which directly bears on F-3's orthogonality framing and H-5's "prefill encodes problem familiarity / decomposability" hypothesis. The paper supplies the strongest missing baseline our selective-prediction work currently lacks.

**Key claim we tested:** Pairwise linguistic confidence elicitation, with no access to log-probs or internal states, can match or exceed supervised internal probes on selective-classification AUC and AUROC. Their Algorithm 1 + TrueSkill is the strongest internals-free baseline against our F-2 / F-8 / H-12.

**Our result:** **TO TEST.** Currently no MATH-500 / Qwen-1.5B replication of their method exists in the project. P11-FE373 (relative-confidence on cached MATH-500 answers), P11-FE374 (difficulty-only variant + correlation with prefill DoM), and P11-FE375 (3-way bake-off vs SEP and supervised DoM) are queued. Outcome dictates whether F-2 / F-8 are reframed and whether H-12's SEP framing is replaced with relative-confidence.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE373, P11-FE374, P11-FE375, P11-FE376; H-299, H-300, H-301

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **Pairwise relative confidence prompting (Algorithm 1)** — for each q_i, randomly sample n peers q_j from the same dataset and ask "which are you more confident in?" Greedy T=0 generations.
  *Replication cost*: ~30 min CPU per dataset for the prompt-construction loop; cost dominated by API/model calls (15×500 = 7500 inferences for one MATH-500 sweep at n=15). On a local Qwen-1.5B this is ~1h H100.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **yes** — it's the strongest missing baseline against F-2/F-8 and we already have all 500 MATH-500 generations cached.

- **Difficulty-only prompt (Section 5)** — same pairwise format but answers are *withheld*; model judges which question is harder.
  *Replication cost*: same as above, additional 7500 calls.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **yes** — directly tests F-3's reframing (refutation #3) and H-5's difficulty-encoding hypothesis. High-leverage.

- **Elo rating aggregation** — K=400, init=1000, n_iters tuned in [1, 20]; iterative online update on shuffled match list.
  *Replication cost*: <1 min CPU, pure-numpy.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — small.

- **TrueSkill aggregation** — μ=25, σ=μ/3, β=μ/6, τ=μ/300; uses `trueskill` PyPI package; Bayesian skill posterior.
  *Replication cost*: <1 min CPU.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — best-performing aggregator on most models, recommended starting point.

- **Bradley-Terry MLE aggregation** — log-likelihood + L2 (λ=0.01), BFGS optimizer; max-iters tuned in [1, 20].
  *Replication cost*: <1 min CPU.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — sanity check against TrueSkill.

- **CoT-augmented confidence preference (Section 5, negative result)** — adds explicit reasoning to the comparison prompt; AUC drops from 87.2 to 86.8 on GPT-4o due to confabulated evidence.
  *Replication cost*: same as relative-confidence + CoT generation cost.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **no** — paper itself reports negative result; not worth re-replicating unless cross-checking the failure mode.

- **Selective-classification AUC with Gaussian-noise tie-breaking** — the confidence score gets ε-noise added to break ties when many examples share scores. Important detail for any selective-classification metric we report.
  *Replication cost*: trivial.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: **yes** — should adopt for our F-8 reporting; we don't currently document tie-handling.

### Approaches & framings

- **Confidence-as-rank-aggregation reframe.** Confidence estimation reframed as a noisy / inconsistent / incomplete pairwise-comparison problem solvable by rank aggregation. Intersects F-8 directly: if confidence is fundamentally relative, our supervised DoM probe (which produces an absolute scalar per example) is solving a strictly harder problem than necessary. Suggests reformulating F-8 as a rank-prediction task ("can the DoM correctly order pairs by P(correct)?") rather than a calibration task.

- **Difficulty as a separable component of confidence.** The Section-5 difficulty-only result implies confidence ≈ difficulty(question) + answer-conditional-signal. This separation is testable in our pipeline by regressing prefill DoM scores on (a) a difficulty proxy and (b) an answer-quality proxy. Bears on H-5 (familiarity vs decomposability) and reframes F-3.

- **"Models are better at relative judgments than absolute" (cited from Kadavath 2022).** Generalization of the well-known LLM-as-judge finding that pairwise > pointwise. Suggests our ABC-44 / D-bucket classifier framing should be tested as a pairwise problem (is question A more likely to be in D-bucket than question B?) rather than absolute classification.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **GPQA** (Rein 2023) — 250 test examples used; HF dataset, public. Applicable? **partial** — high difficulty but multiple-choice not free-form math; doesn't match our 1024-tok MATH-500 regime directly.
- **MedQA** (Jin 2021) — 250 test examples; HF, public. Applicable? **no** — domain shift away from math reasoning.
- **TruthfulQA** (Lin 2021) — 250 test examples; HF, public. Applicable? **no** — knowledge/factuality, not reasoning.
- **CommonsenseQA, OpenbookQA, SIQA** — HF, public. Applicable? **no** — commonsense, off-topic for our math-reasoning probe.
- **MMLU** subsets (8: law, ethics, conceptual physics, econometrics, abstract algebra, college chemistry, computer security, US foreign policy) — 250 examples each; HF, public. Applicable? **partial** — abstract algebra and conceptual physics overlap with MATH topics; the rest are knowledge MCQ.

The project's MATH-500 benchmark is *not* in their evaluation set — direct comparison requires running their method on MATH-500 ourselves. They use MCQ format throughout; MATH-500 is free-form numerical answers, so the pairwise comparison prompt would need to be adapted (compare two solved problems and pick which the model is more confident in).

### Implementation details worth capturing

- **Greedy T=0 for the answer + confidence; T=0.7 for self-consistency baseline (15 samples).** Don't mix temperatures across the pipeline.
- **n=15 pairwise comparisons per question** is the saturation point for GPT-4o (Table 2: gains plateau at 1.8% from n=10→n=15). For Llama-405B still climbing at n=15 (4.9%). Plan for at least n=15 on Qwen-1.5B; consider n=30 to check saturation on a smaller model.
- **Hyperparameters (Table 8 fixed defaults)**: Elo K=400, init=1000, 1 iter; TrueSkill μ=25, σ=μ/3, β=μ/6, τ=μ/300; Bradley-Terry max-iter 5, λ=0.01.
- **Min-max normalization** applied to final aggregated scores → [0, 1] range. Don't compare raw Elo / TrueSkill scores across runs without this normalization.
- **Tie-breaking via Gaussian noise** added to confidences for AUC computation (their footnote on Shrivastava 2023). Not in our current `validate_claims.py` selective-prediction code.
- **`trueskill` PyPI package** is the recommended TrueSkill implementation. Bradley-Terry uses `scipy.optimize.minimize` with BFGS.
- **No code link in paper** — would need to re-implement Algorithms 1–3 from pseudocode (small).

### Replicable intermediates

- **Pairwise-relative-confidence on cached MATH-500 / Qwen-1.5B answers.** The MATH-500 K=1 answers are already in `pathway11_h100/prefill_gated_compute/results.json` (243/500 correct, F-2 source). Loop pairwise prompts on Qwen-1.5B over these 500 questions+answers (n=15), aggregate via TrueSkill, compute AUROC against the 5-fold OOF split. ~1h H100. Smallest-cross-check version: subsample to 100 questions, n=10 → ~10 min H100. **This is the single most informative experiment from this triage.**
- **Difficulty-only variant**: same as above but withhold answers in prompt. Same cost.
- **Difficulty proxy correlation with prefill DoM scores**: regress prefill DoM scalars (from the cached F-2 NPZ) on difficulty-only scores from the variant above. Pure-CPU after the difficulty scores exist.

### Cross-paper signals

- **2306.13063** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Xiong et al. self-consistency confidence elicitation is the direct absolute-confidence baseline this paper outperforms; our project's selective-prediction work would benefit from having it as a comparator alongside SEP.
- **2311.08877** — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Shrivastava 2023 ("Llamas know what GPTs don't show") is the direct predecessor and supplies the absolute-confidence prompt + tie-breaking-noise convention this paper inherits. Specifically relevant to F-8's selective-classification metric definition.
- **2406.15927** (Semantic Entropy Probes) — already in graph as CITED ONLY (motivates H-12). Direct competitor to relative-confidence as a label-free baseline.
- **2410.13640** (Chain-of-Embedding) — already in graph (PARTIALLY CONFIRMED / CONTRADICTED). Tangentially related: CoE uses internal trajectory features for confidence, this paper uses external pairwise prompts — orthogonal axes of the "confidence elicitation" design space.
- **2402.01306** (KTO) — NOT in graph; flagged in their Future Work. Low priority for our project (alignment, not confidence).
- **2305.18290** (DPO) — NOT in graph; flagged in their Future Work. Out of scope.
- **2604.22271** (Kumaran 2026, internal confidence signals for self-correction) — already in graph as TO TEST. Internal-signal counterpart to this paper's external-elicitation framing — together they bracket the "label-free confidence" design space.

## 2502.01657 — Improving Rule-based Reasoning in LLMs using Neurosymbolic Representations (Dhanraj & Eliasmith, 2025)

**Relevance:** Paper trains a linear encoder/decoder pair at LLaMA-3.1-8B layer 17 to map hidden states into a Holographic Reduced Representation (HRR) vector-symbolic algebra space, performs symbolic computation in that space, and writes the solution back into the residual stream via 50/50 mixing — gated by a 0.8 dot-product similarity threshold for OOD refusal. They report 88.6% lower CE loss and 15.4× more correct answers on a procedurally generated single-token arithmetic benchmark vs. CoT and LoRA baselines. The work is directly relevant to F-2 (single-layer privileged for hidden-state probing), F-3 (deeper-layer scrambling via residual+RMS), F-9 (single-layer sufficiency), and re-opens H-1 by demonstrating that single-layer fixed-α intervention works when the inserted vector is per-prompt-computed.

**Key claim we tested:** A linear encoder at a specific mid-late layer can recover structured problem-input information (digit-level, operation-type) with <2% per-digit error, and a linear decoder with 50/50 mixing at the same layer can write back a *solution* that the rest of the LLM completes correctly.

**Our result:** **TO TEST** — paper's results not yet replicated on Qwen-2.5-1.5B. Their L17/32 layer choice in LLaMA-3.1-8B is at a comparable depth fraction to our L19/28 in Qwen, but their criterion (problem-input reconstruction RMSE) differs from ours (correctness AUROC). The direct cross-checks are H-302 (does the layer choice transfer when target changes from problem-input to problem-type), H-303 (does per-prompt single-layer steering work when the source vector is correctness-direction rather than VSA-solution), and H-304 (do structured probes beat scalar DoM).

**Related experiments:** P11-FE377, P11-FE378, P11-FE379, P11-FE380, H-302, H-303, H-304.

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **HRR-VSA encoding of hidden states** — train a linear encoder `h → v ∈ R^2048` whose target is a structured Holographic Reduced Representation `v = bind(n1, hundreds⊗d2 + tens⊗d1 + ones⊗d0) + bind(n2, …) + bind(problem_type, op)`, then a linear decoder `v → h` that maps a *solution* VSA vector back to a hidden state. Encoder/decoder both linear, RMSE loss, 1000 epochs, then 1 epoch of CE fine-tune on LLM logits.
  *Replication cost*: ~4h on a single 8B-class GPU per layer; encoder/decoder are tiny linear maps so negligible compute. The harder part is choosing what symbolic targets to bind for *non-arithmetic* problems (MATH-500 is not just digit arithmetic).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes, but only the linear-probe-with-structured-targets variant. Full HRR over MATH-500 isn't worth the targets-design cost. The 0.8 dot-product gating mechanism is portable.

- **Linear-encoder layer sweep with reconstruction RMSE** — train an encoder per layer, plot RMSE vs layer, pick the minimum. Their Figure 2 shows RMSE bottoms out at L17 then rises with depth.
  *Replication cost*: 30min CPU on cached Qwen 1.5B Stage-2 NPZs.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly tests the F-2 layer-specificity claim (proposed FE below).

- **50/50 hidden-state intervention with similarity gating** — at the chosen layer, replace `h ← 0.5·h + 0.5·decoder(VSA_solution)` only when `dot(encoded_VSA, problem_type_proto) > 0.8`. Otherwise pass through unchanged. This is a *learned-vector* version of P10 fixed-α steering with an explicit refusal mechanism on OOD inputs.
  *Replication cost*: tiny; the inference loop modification is trivial.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly relevant to H-1 un-parking (proposed FE below).

- **Procedurally-generated single-token-answer arithmetic benchmark** — Symbolic-Math: 20k train / 200 val / 2000 test, 10 problem types (mod, ×, gcd, lcm, x²mod, AND, XOR, OR, +, //), all answers truncated to single LLaMA tokens via mod-1000.
  *Replication cost*: trivial generation, MIT-licensed.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: maybe — useful as a *toy domain* for testing whether F-2 / F-7 generalise off MATH-500 onto a fully synthetic single-step rule-following benchmark.

### Approaches & framings

- **Hidden states carry compositionally decodable problem inputs at a specific mid-late layer.** This reframes the L19/L17 phenomenon: it's not about *correctness* per se, it's about *problem features being maximally linearly available* before deep mixing scrambles them. This is a *decoupling* of "where is the problem state most legible" from "where does the model decide whether to be right".
- **Symbolic-space offload as steering.** Recasts intervention not as "push along a direction" but as "round-trip through a structured external representation, edit there, write back". Suggests our P10 framework may have been too narrow — the right intervention may be a per-prompt-computed *displacement vector* rather than a global direction.
- **OOD refusal via similarity gating.** Their threshold mechanism makes the steering operation *self-suspending* on out-of-distribution inputs. This is a constructive design pattern for any steering method we might revive — gate on probe confidence, refuse intervention otherwise.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **Symbolic-Math Dataset** (introduced by paper) — 22.2k examples, 10 arithmetic operations on 3-digit ints, single-token answers, MIT licensed, fully procedurally regenerable, GitHub at vdhanraj/Symbolic-Math-Dataset. Applicable? yes (limited) — useful as a *controlled* toy domain to ask whether F-2 / F-9 are MATH-500-specific or generalise to pure arithmetic.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- LLaMA-3.1 8B, 32 layers, 4096-dim hidden states; intervention at layer 17.
- VSA dimensionality: 2048 (chosen to match the LoRA rank baseline so trainable-param count is comparable).
- Encoder + decoder: linear maps. RMSE loss. 1000 epochs of pre-training + 1 epoch of CE fine-tune on LLM logits.
- Mixing ratio: 50/50 between decoder output and original hidden state. Justified empirically in Appendix D (not read).
- Similarity gating threshold: 0.8 dot product against problem-type prototypes.
- Few-shot prompting: 2 in-context exemplars per query. Greedy decoding (T=0).
- HRR binding = circular convolution; bundling = vector addition; similarity = dot product.
- Pseudo-inverse for unbinding: `y† = (y_1, y_d, y_{d-1}, …, y_2)`.
- Code: github.com/vdhanraj/Neurosymbolic-LLM and github.com/vdhanraj/Symbolic-Math-Dataset.
- Compute overhead: Θ(d·v + v·log v) per forward pass, dominated by the standard transformer cost — negligible.

### Replicable intermediates

- **Layer-sweep RMSE for problem-type linear probe on Qwen 1.5B**: train a per-layer linear classifier on cached Stage-2 NPZs (`pathway11_h100/cache/`) targeting MATH-500 sub-problem-type labels (algebra/geometry/number-theory/probability/etc., already in the MATH-500 metadata). Plot accuracy vs layer. Predicts: peak should be near L19 if F-2's layer is universal across information types; peak elsewhere refutes the L19-specificity claim.
- **Replicate paper's headline on Qwen**: re-run their public code on Qwen-2.5-1.5B at L19 with the Symbolic-Math dataset. If their 95%+ accuracy on mod/×/AND/XOR/OR replicates on Qwen, the method is portable; if not, LLaMA-3.1-specific.
- **Per-prompt steering mock-up**: take the cached Pathway-11 prefill DoM scores, train a tiny MLP `prefill_h_L19 → predicted_correctness` then an inverse mapping back into hidden-state space, splice at L19, see if accuracy moves. Cheap (1 hour CPU) test of refutation #2.

### Cross-paper signals

- 2410.05229 — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Mirzadeh et al. *GSM-Symbolic* — directly tests rule-following fragility in arithmetic. Cited by paper as motivation. Connects to F-7 (D-bucket fragility) and H-9 (breathing predicts difficulty).
- 2406.06588 — NOT in graph; recommend admission. Petruzzellis et al. on assessing LLaMA's emergent symbolic reasoning. Same problem space; would inform H-22 (abstract-CoT) and H-5 (problem familiarity).
- 2412.04604 — NOT in graph; not worth admission unless we pivot to ARC-prize-style abstract reasoning. Cited as program-synthesis comparator.
- 2305.12295 — NOT in graph; LogicLM (LLM + symbolic solver). Conceptual cousin; not core to our findings.
- 2402.00854 — NOT in graph; SymbolicAI framework. Same: peripheral.
- 2310.15164 — NOT in graph; LINC neurosymbolic logic. Peripheral.
- 2407.21783 — NOT in graph; LLaMA-3 herd-of-models tech report. Reference only; not worth admission.

## 2502.03407 — Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes (Goldowsky-Dill, Chughtai, Heimersheim, Hobbhahn / Apollo Research, 2025)

**Relevance:** The paper evaluates linear probes on residual-stream activations of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct for detecting strategic deception, achieving AUROC 0.96–0.999. The task is structurally analogous to our correctness prediction: both are binary classifications over model outputs using early-middle-layer linear probes. The primary relevance is (1) as an empirical upper-bound reference showing that single-layer linear probes can saturate for related tasks, contextualizing our 0.7731 AUROC (F-2); (2) as a methodological comparison showing LR ≈ DoM for in-distribution discrimination but LR > DoM when the control distribution is far from training; and (3) as a direct demonstration of the domain-contamination failure mode that F-2's "strongest counterargument" already flags (H-5).

**Key claim we tested:** Single-layer logistic regression probes on residual-stream activations can detect strategic deception with AUROC 0.96–0.999, generalizing from simple contrastive training data to realistic high-stakes deception scenarios (insider trading, sandbagging).

**Our result:** **TO TEST** The paper's AUROC values (0.96–0.999 for deception) bound the ceiling for our correctness task (0.7731 for F-2). We have not tested whether (a) a layer sweep improves on 0.7731, or (b) our AUROC degrades within matched subject strata (domain contamination). P11-FE381 and H-305 lay out these two tests.

**Related experiments:** P11-FE381, H-305, H-5, F-2, F-9

**Status:** TO TEST

### Methodologies extracted

- **Logistic regression probe on residual stream** — l2-regularized (λ=10) logistic regression on zero-mean, unit-variance normalized activations; flattened across samples × token positions; probe weight vector defines the direction.
  *Replication cost*: 20min CPU.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — we already use this approach for DoM in F-2; this paper validates the method and adds λ=10 as a calibrated default.

- **Instructed-Pairs contrastive training** — pairs of activations that differ only in an honest/deceptive instruction prefix; the model's response text is held constant. Targets the *intent* dimension before any behavioral signal appears.
  *Replication cost*: ~2h to construct pairs + 20min CPU to train.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes, for a "correctness-intent" version — construct correct-instruction vs incorrect-instruction paired prompts and probe the resulting direction. Potentially cleaner than labeling outputs.

- **Per-layer AUROC sweep** — same probe trained independently at each layer; swept against held-out validation set to select optimal layer.
  *Replication cost*: ~2h CPU on cached NPZs (28 layers × 500 problems).
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes — directly motivated by R2; would either validate L19 or find a better layer.

- **Mean vs max aggregation of per-token scores** — alternatives to simple mean (max, ReLU-threshold mean) for aggregating per-token probe scores to a per-response classification.
  *Replication cost*: 5min CPU.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes, cheap post-hoc on existing Stage 2 per-token activations.

- **Follow-up question probing** — insert "Was your last response deceptive? (Yes/No)" after each response, gather activations at the "No" response token, train probe on those activations.
  *Replication cost*: H100 day to regenerate activations for MATH-500 with follow-up prompts.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: no — specific to deception detection; not directly applicable to correctness, where the follow-up would be "Was your answer correct?" (model often outputs "Yes" regardless).

- **SAE-based probe comparison** — replace raw residual activations with Sparse Autoencoder feature activations before logistic regression; compare generalization performance.
  *Replication cost*: 4h CPU if SAE weights are available for Qwen-2.5-1.5B.
  *We'd plausibly run this*: yes, as a falsification test for H-12 / R3.

### Approaches & framings

**Probe activation ≠ probe classification**: The paper separates "AUROC for deceptive vs honest" from "recall at 1% FPR on control" as two distinct performance metrics. For our correctness prediction task, the analogous split is "AUROC on MATH-500 balanced classes" vs "precision at fixed coverage on deployment distribution." This framing maps directly to our selective-prediction setup (F-8, 71.6% at 50% coverage) and suggests evaluating our probe against a held-out "neutral" math-adjacent distribution to measure control-vs-deceptive gap. Intersects F-8, H-9.

**Generalization gap as a probe quality metric**: The paper frames generalization from Instructed-Pairs (simple contrastive instructions) to realistic deception scenarios as the key test of probe quality. Our DoM generalizes from MATH-500 to BBH (AUROC ~0.7199 per F-9); the paper suggests that probes trained on abstracted contrastive pairs (rather than in-distribution trajectories) tend to generalize better. Suggests an alternative DoM construction via instruction-contrasting rather than outcome-labeling. Intersects F-2, F-9, H-5.

### Datasets & benchmarks

- **Roleplaying dataset** (custom, Apollo Research, inspired by Pacchiardi et al. 2023) — 371 responses (84 honest / 84 ambiguous / 203 deceptive); low-realism scenarios. Not released publicly (appears to be at data.apolloresearch.ai). Applicable? no — MATH-500 regime; but the construction method (GPT-4o-generated scenarios with strategic lie incentives) is replicable.

- **Insider Trading dataset** (Scheurer et al. 2023) — 1329 responses (669/324/336); high-realism AI-assistant-under-pressure scenarios. Applicable? no — but the sandbagging variant (deliberate incorrect answers under instruction) has a structural parallel to our D-bucket analysis (F-7).

- **Sandbagging dataset** (Benton et al. 2024) — 995 responses on WMDP (harmful) vs MMLU (neutral) questions; model instructed to deliberately fail WMDP. Applicable? partial — if we want a probe that detects "model is deliberately giving wrong answers" vs "model genuinely doesn't know," this dataset structure would apply. Not accessible as a standalone download.

- **Alpaca** (Taori et al. 2023) — 9,994 Llama responses to instruction-following queries; used as control to calibrate false positive rate. Applicable? yes — we could use Alpaca responses as a control distribution for measuring our correctness probe's FPR on non-math queries. HF: tatsu-lab/alpaca. Accessible: yes.

### Implementation details worth capturing

- Layer 22 of 80 in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct was chosen by sweep on Llama-3.1-70B and found to transfer to Llama-3.3; ~27% depth. Note our L19 is ~68% depth in 28-layer model — opposite regime.
- Logistic regression with `l2` penalty and `λ=10` (i.e., `C=0.1` in sklearn's convention); normalization: zero mean, unit variance on training set, applied identically to test.
- Flatten across samples and token positions before fitting (each token position is a training sample with the response-level label).
- Mean aggregation across token positions to produce per-response score.
- Code: https://github.com/ApolloResearch/deception-detection
- Data viewer: https://data.apolloresearch.ai/dd/

### Replicable intermediates

- **Layer sweep on Stage 2 NPZs**: We have cached per-layer activations for all 28 Qwen-2.5-1.5B layers from P11 H100 Stage 2 extraction. Running `sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression(C=0.1, max_iter=1000)` on each layer's L19-equivalent mean-pooled activations takes ~2h CPU. Compares each layer's 5-fold OOF AUROC against our 0.7731 baseline. Script: add a layer loop to existing `pathway11_h100/` probe scripts.

- **Per-subject AUROC stratification on MATH-500**: MATH-500 has labeled subject categories (algebra, number theory, geometry, counting & probability, precalculus, prealgebra). We can filter `results.json` by problem subject and compute AUROC within each stratum using the existing prefill DoM score column. No new extraction needed. Script: ~50 lines against cached `results.json`. Directly tests R1.
